items.title: Simandou Mining Summit : Mamadi Doumbouya définit les contours de la nouvelle vision économique guinéenne (Par Oumar Kateb Yacine)
items.description: La première édition du Simandou Mining Summit, tenue du 11 au 13 novembre 2026 à Kassa et à Conakry, a réuni 2 240 participants venus de 41 pays. Au-delà des enjeux miniers, cette rencontre internationale ambitionne de positionner la Guinée comme un acteur majeur de la transformation économique. À l’ouverture des travaux, le président Mamadi Doumbouya a exposé sa vision d’une Guinée économiquement souveraine, résolument tournée vers l’industrialisation, la transformation locale de ses ressources et la diversification de ses partenariats. Il y a des discours qui se limitent à annoncer des ambitions. D’autres cherchent à fixer un cap et à inscrire une nation dans une nouvelle trajectoire historique. Depuis l’île de Kassa, face à l’Atlantique, le 11 novembre, le président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, a voulu donner à la première édition du Simandou Mining Summit une dimension qui dépasse largement le cadre d’une rencontre consacrée à l’industrie minière. Son intervention a surtout porté un message politique et économique sans ambiguïté. La Guinée entend désormais être davantage actrice de son développement, maîtresse de ses ressources et partie prenante des décisions qui engagent son avenir. Le choix de Kassa pour accueillir cette rencontre n’est pas anodin. Un an après le départ du premier minerai de fer de Simandou depuis le port de Moribaya, le chef de l’État a rappelé la portée historique de cette réalisation, longtemps considérée comme l’un des grands rendez-vous manqués de l’économie guinéenne. « Pendant des décennies, Simandou fut le symbole des occasions manquées », a-t-il rappelé, avant de souligner le changement intervenu dans la conduite de ce projet stratégique. « Ensemble, nous l’avons fait. Une mine, un chemin de fer transguinéen, un port minéralier et commercial. La chaîne est en marche, et elle ne s’arrêtera plus. » Cette déclaration résume une première rupture. Celle d’un pays qui ne veut plus se satisfaire de son immense potentiel géologique, mais qui entend démontrer sa capacité à transformer ses ressources naturelles en réalisations concrètes. Simandou n’est donc plus seulement un gisement de minerai de fer. Il devient le symbole d’une nouvelle méthode de gouvernance économique, fondée sur la réalisation des projets structurants, la mobilisation des investissements et la maîtrise des infrastructures stratégiques. Simandou, bien plus qu’un projet minier Mais le message essentiel du président Doumbouya réside dans sa volonté de ne pas enfermer l’avenir économique du pays dans la seule exploitation du minerai de fer. Le projet Simandou constitue, dans sa vision, un levier de transformation beaucoup plus vaste, appelé à irriguer plusieurs secteurs de l’économie nationale. « Simandou n’est pas une fin. C’est une porte », a-t-il affirmé. Une formule courte, mais particulièrement révélatrice de la philosophie qui sous-tend le programme Simandou 2040. Cette vision repose sur une conviction fondamentale. Les ressources minières ne doivent pas constituer une richesse isolée, concentrée dans quelques activités extractives, mais servir de moteur à l’industrialisation, à la création d’emplois, au développement des infrastructures, à la formation professionnelle et à la diversification du tissu productif. C’est précisément le sens de cette ambition présidentielle lorsqu’il affirme que « chaque richesse extraite de notre sol laisse en République de Guinée du travail, de la formation, des entreprises et de la dignité ». Derrière cette déclaration se dessine une nouvelle conception de la politique minière. L’exploitation des ressources naturelles doit désormais être appréciée non seulement à travers les volumes de production et les recettes d’exportation, mais aussi par sa capacité à générer des activités économiques sur le territoire national. La transformation locale devient ainsi un impératif stratégique. Pendant trop longtemps, la Guinée a exporté une part importante de ses richesses sous forme de matières premières, laissant à d’autres économies le soin de capter une partie substantielle de la valeur ajoutée industrielle. Cette logique, le président entend progressivement la dépasser. « La Guinée ne se contentera plus d’exporter ses ressources à l’état brut. Elle les transformera chez elle », a-t-il martelé. L’annonce de la perspective d’une aciérie destinée à transformer le fer de Simandou sur le sol guinéen s’inscrit dans cette orientation. Elle traduit la volonté de franchir un nouveau palier, celui de l’industrialisation, où les ressources naturelles deviennent les matières premières d’une économie productive et créatrice de valeur. La souveraineté économique comme nouvelle doctrine L’un des aspects les plus significatifs de cette intervention présidentielle concerne la souveraineté économique. Il ne s’agit pas, dans le discours de Kassa, de remettre en cause l’ouverture de la Guinée aux investissements étrangers. Il s’agit plutôt de redéfinir les conditions dans lesquelles ces investissements doivent contribuer au développement national. La différence est fondamentale. Une économie ouverte ne signifie pas une économie qui renonce à ses intérêts stratégiques. La Guinée entend accueillir les investisseurs, mais dans un cadre où les intérêts de l’État, les retombées pour les populations et le développement des entreprises nationales occupent une place centrale. Cette orientation se traduit notamment par la mise en avant de nouveaux instruments institutionnels et économiques. La Compagnie du TransGuinéen, appelée à ouvrir les infrastructures à différents opérateurs dans des conditions d’équité, illustre cette volonté de faire des équipements structurants un levier collectif de développement. La Nimba Mining Company, quant à elle, porte l’ambition de faire émerger un acteur minier guinéen de premier plan. À cela s’ajoute la mise en service annoncée de la Nimba Gold Refinery, ainsi que l’émergence de projets de raffineries d’alumine. Ces initiatives participent d’une même logique. Il ne suffit plus de disposer de ressources abondantes et d’attirer des capitaux. Il faut également renforcer les capacités nationales, développer les compétences locales et favoriser l’émergence d’entreprises capables de prendre une part croissante dans la chaîne de valeur minière. La souveraineté économique ne se proclame donc pas uniquement dans les discours. Elle se construit à travers les infrastructures, les institutions, la formation, l’industrialisation et la capacité de l’État à négocier des partenariats qui servent durablement l’intérêt national. Une Guinée ouverte, mais désormais plus exigeante sur ses partenariats Autre message fort du discours de Kassa, la volonté de diversifier les partenariats économiques. Dans un environnement international marqué par la compétition pour les ressources stratégiques, la Guinée dispose d’un atout considérable. Son potentiel minier, sa position géographique et les perspectives ouvertes par Simandou lui donnent une capacité de négociation qu’elle entend pleinement valoriser. Le président Mamadi Doumbouya a clairement exprimé cette posture devant les investisseurs présents au sommet. « La Guinée ne tend pas la main. Elle ouvre les bras. » Cette formule mérite une attention particulière. Elle traduit le passage d’une logique de dépendance à une logique de partenariat. Le pays ne se présente pas comme un demandeur de faveur, mais comme un partenaire disposant d’atouts économiques, de ressources stratégiques et d’une vision de développement. Le chef de l’État a d’ailleurs précisé les fondements de cette nouvelle approche en déclarant que la Guinée ne demandait « ni faveur ni charité », mais proposait « un partenariat d’égal à égal, fondé sur le respect de la parole donnée et le partage équitable de la valeur ». Cette position ouvre la voie à une diversification des partenaires, sans exclusive géographique ou politique. La Guinée doit pouvoir travailler avec tous les pays et tous les investisseurs disposés à respecter ses priorités économiques, ses intérêts stratégiques et ses exigences en matière de retombées nationales. Il ne s’agit donc pas de substituer un partenaire à un autre, ni de déplacer une dépendance économique vers une nouvelle sphère d’influence. L’enjeu est plutôt de multiplier les possibilités de coopération, de renforcer la concurrence entre les investisseurs et de donner à l’État guinéen une plus grande marge de manœuvre dans la négociation des accords. Cette diversification constitue l’un des fondements d’une souveraineté économique véritable. Car un pays qui dispose de plusieurs partenaires crédibles et de différentes options de coopération est mieux placé pour défendre ses intérêts et construire des relations équilibrées. Simandou 2040, le pari de la transformation nationale La portée du sommet de Kassa se mesure également à l’aune du programme Simandou 2040. Celui-ci entend faire du projet minier le catalyseur d’une transformation économique et sociale de grande ampleur. Les secteurs évoqués par le président sont révélateurs de cette ambition. Aux mines s’ajoutent l’énergie, l’agriculture, la logistique, le numérique et le tourisme. Autant de domaines dont le développement doit permettre à la Guinée de sortir progressivement d’une économie excessivement dépendante des industries extractives. Cette diversification est une nécessité. L’expérience de nombreux pays producteurs de matières premières montre que l’abondance des ressources naturelles ne garantit pas automatiquement la prospérité. Sans industrialisation, sans infrastructures adaptées, sans investissement dans le capital humain et sans développement du secteur privé, les richesses du sous-sol peuvent coexister avec des difficultés économiques et sociales persistantes. C’est pourquoi le président a insisté sur la place de la jeunesse dans cette nouvelle dynamique, en mettant notamment en avant la Simandou Academy. La formation des compétences nationales constitue en effet une condition essentielle pour que les Guinéens ne soient pas de simples spectateurs des transformations économiques annoncées, mais des acteurs directs de leur réalisation. La question de l’emploi, du transfert de compétences et de la participation des entreprises locales devra ainsi occuper une place centrale dans l’évaluation des retombées du programme. Le véritable succès de Simandou ne se mesurera pas uniquement au tonnage de minerai exporté, aux kilomètres de voies ferrées construits ou aux investissements mobilisés. Il se mesurera aussi à la capacité de ces réalisations à améliorer durablement les conditions de vie des populations, à renforcer le tissu industriel et à ouvrir de nouvelles perspectives aux générations futures. Un rendez-vous avec l’histoire, mais surtout avec les résultats En décidant de suivre personnellement les travaux du sommet, le président Mamadi Doumbouya a également voulu envoyer un signal aux investisseurs et aux partenaires économiques. « Je suivrai personnellement vos travaux, afin que les partenariats, les projets et les décisions qui en naîtront se concrétisent », a-t-il assuré. Cette volonté de suivi traduit une préoccupation essentielle. La crédibilité d’une politique économique se construit dans la continuité entre les engagements, les décisions et leur exécution. Les rencontres internationales n’ont de véritable portée que lorsqu’elles débouchent sur des projets financés, des investissements réalisés et des résultats mesurables. Le rendez-vous annoncé dans deux ans pour rendre compte des avancées donne à cette première édition du Simandou Mining Summit une dimension supplémentaire. Il engage les autorités guinéennes à inscrire les ambitions présentées à Kassa dans une dynamique de responsabilité et de résultats. C’est dire que le discours du 11 novembre marque une étape importante dans la présentation de la nouvelle vision économique de la Guinée. Il affirme une ambition qui ne se limite pas à faire du pays un grand producteur minier, mais à le positionner comme un acteur capable de transformer ses ressources, de diversifier ses partenariats et de construire une prospérité fondée sur la création de valeur nationale. Longtemps présentée comme un scandale géologique, la Guinée veut désormais démontrer qu’elle peut devenir un modèle de transformation économique. Le défi reste immense. Il suppose de la rigueur dans la gouvernance, de la constance dans les politiques publiques, une meilleure articulation entre les investissements et les besoins des populations, ainsi qu’une capacité permanente à préserver l’équilibre entre ouverture internationale et intérêts nationaux. Mais une conviction se dégage du discours présidentiel. Le temps où la richesse du sous-sol constituait une promesse sans lendemain doit céder la place à celui où elle devient un instrument de développement. À Kassa, Mamadi Doumbouya a résumé cette ambition en quelques mots qui sonnent comme un appel aux investisseurs et un engagement envers les Guinéens. « Le moment de la Guinée, c’est maintenant. » Oumar Kateb Yacine Journaliste et Analyste géopolitique Contact : bahoumaryacine777@gmail.com L’article Simandou Mining Summit : Mamadi Doumbouya définit les contours de la nouvelle vision économique guinéenne (Par Oumar Kateb Yacine) est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Enseignement supérieur : El Midaoui écarte l'intégration directe des docteurs du privé
items.description: L'intégration des enseignants titulaires d'un doctorat exerçant dans le secteur privé au sein des universités publiques ne se fera pas en dehors des procédures ordinaires de recrutement. Interrogé sur cette revendication, qui concerne quelque 200 docteurs ayant notamment acquis une expérience dans les universités marocaines, le ministre de l'Enseignement supérieur, de la recherche scientifique et de l'innovation, Azzedine El Midaoui, a réaffirmé le principe du recrutement par concours, ouvert à l’ensemble des titulaires d’un doctorat, indépendamment de leur situation professionnelle ou de leur établissement d’origine. Lors du point de presse tenu ce jeudi 19 novembre à l'issue du Conseil de gouvernement, il a également détaillé les principales dispositions du nouveau décret relatif au statut des enseignants de l'enseignement supérieur. © Mounir Mehimdate Pour justifier cette position, le ministre est revenu sur les raisons ayant conduit à la préparation du nouveau statut des enseignants de l’enseignement supérieur. Le précédent texte remontait à 1997, avant l’adoption d’un nouveau statut en 2023. Mais ces dispositifs ont laissé subsister plusieurs situations particulières, sources de difficultés pour certaines catégories d’enseignants. Il a notamment cité le cas des titulaires de doctorats français, une question soulevée depuis près de trente ans et régulièrement portée par les deux syndicats représentant les enseignants de l’enseignement supérieur. Le nouveau décret vise, selon lui, à apporter une réponse à ces situations et à résoudre notamment cette difficulté, dans le cadre d’une concertation avec les organisations syndicales. Le texte entend également corriger les disparités dont étaient victimes les enseignants issus d’autres établissements de formation des cadres, mis à la disposition des universités puis intégrés à leurs structures. Ces derniers étaient notamment confrontés à des inégalités en matière de promotion. Les ajustements introduits doivent désormais leur garantir le même statut et la même position que les autres enseignants de l’enseignement supérieur. Autre modification évoquée par le ministre : celle des modalités de répartition des quotas de promotion. En vertu de l’article 9 du statut de 2023, ces quotas étaient fixés à l’échelle des présidences d’université. Le nouveau dispositif prévoit désormais leur répartition au niveau de chaque établissement, pris individuellement. Une évolution qui devrait, selon El Midaoui, accroître le nombre d’enseignants susceptibles de bénéficier d’une promotion de grade. © Mounir Mehimdate Les concours comme principe d’égalité S’agissant plus précisément des docteurs travaillant dans le privé, le ministre a rappelé que la fonction publique devait rester ouverte à toutes les catégories, conformément aux principes d’équité et aux droits constitutionnels. Il a, dans ce contexte, évoqué l’ancien mécanisme des « postes de transformation », qui permettait notamment de convertir certains postes, mais qui a disparu depuis 2021. Désormais, a-t-il insisté, le recrutement doit passer par des concours ouverts dans les mêmes conditions à tous les titulaires d’un doctorat, qu’ils exercent déjà dans l’enseignement supérieur, dans un autre établissement public ou au sein d’un ministère. Le ministre a affirmé qu’une proportion non négligeable de candidats issus d’autres institutions avait ainsi rejoint l’enseignement supérieur depuis son arrivée à la tête du département, à l’issue de concours ordinaires. À ses yeux, instaurer une voie d’intégration spécifique pour une catégorie de docteurs reviendrait à introduire une forme de discrimination, positive ou négative. Il estime préférable que chaque candidat se présente devant une commission de recrutement et soit évalué selon les mêmes modalités. Les lauréats peuvent ensuite rejoindre l’université, au même titre que les candidats qui ne disposent pas encore d’un emploi dans la fonction publique. El Midaoui a également justifié cette approche par la nécessité de se conformer aux pratiques internationales, affirmant que l’accès aux universités, à travers le monde, repose sur des procédures de recrutement par concours. The post Enseignement supérieur : El Midaoui écarte l'intégration directe des docteurs du privé appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: What is wrong with us: We have filled our houses of worship, so why are we emptying our conscience?
items.description: Across continents and creeds, faith still builds schools, heals the sick and feeds the hungry. Yet in too many places the language of the sacred is being borrowed to dress greed, deception and abuse in the robes of respectability. The question is not whether we believe, but whether our belief still governs what we do on Monday morning. By Ing. Prof. Douglas Boateng, Chartered Director UK | Chartered Engineer UK | Fellow, Institute of Directors UK | Fellow, Ghana Institution of Engineering | Governance, Industrialisation and Supply Chain Strategist | Founder, Boardroom Governance Summit | Founder and Scriber, NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom) A Tale Of Two Worshippers Picture a man who never misses a service, occupies a front-row seat, gives generously when the cameras are rolling, and lectures others eloquently about righteousness. On Monday he quietly inflates a public contract, on Tuesday he delays his workers’ wages, on Wednesday he telephones a well-placed friend to make an inconvenient investigation disappear, and by the weekend he is being honoured from the pulpit for his generosity, with nobody asking where the money came from and somebody even describing his wealth as evidence of divine favour. Now picture a widow persuaded to surrender her modest savings to a self-styled spiritual authority who promises miraculous financial breakthrough. Her money vanishes, her circumstances deteriorate, and she is gently told that perhaps her faith was insufficient, while the beneficiary of her devotion acquires yet another luxury vehicle and she is encouraged simply to pray harder. The Question We Would Rather Not Ask What is wrong with us? How did we arrive at a place where religious appearance can command more respect than moral conduct, and why are we sometimes more offended by someone questioning a religious leader than by credible evidence that the leader may have exploited the very people who trusted him? It is a question that unsettles believers and sceptics alike, which is precisely why it must be asked with humility rather than hostility. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom): When religion becomes a costume for dishonesty, the greatest danger is not the absence of faith but the quiet disappearance of conscience. A Religious World, But Not Necessarily A Righteous One Religion remains one of the most powerful forces in human civilisation. According to the Pew Research Center’s 2025 study of the global religious landscape, about 75.8 per cent of the world’s population identified with a religion in 2020. Yet affiliation is a statement of identity, not a certificate of character. A person can recite sacred texts flawlessly and still exploit employees, while another who professes no faith at all may display remarkable honesty and compassion. The real test of any value system, religious or secular, is whether it shapes our behaviour when nobody is watching and when dishonesty offers a handsome reward. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom): The true measure of righteousness is not how loudly we proclaim our beliefs, but how faithfully we practise justice when injustice would pay us better. Ghana’s Mirror: Full Pews, Leaking Public Purses My own country offers a thought provoking illustration. The 2021 Population and Housing Census found that 71.3 per cent of Ghanaians identify as Christian, 19.9 per cent as Muslim and 3.2 per cent as adherents of African traditional religions. Yet Ghana scored 43 out of 100 on Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, ranking 76th of 182 countries and remaining at roughly that level since 2020, even as illegal mining poisons rivers our grandparents drank from without fear. Religion does not cause these problems, and similar failings are found in far less religious societies. The point is subtler and more uncomfortable: devotion cannot substitute for functioning institutions, personal integrity and standards that are enforced without fear or favour. The worshipper who offers a bribe, the executive who donates lavishly while starving suppliers of payment, and the official who invokes divine guidance while undermining procurement rules are not facing a theological contradiction. Theirs is a behavioural one. Our elders captured our dilemma in a proverb: the cow gave birth to fire; if she licks it, it burns her, and if she abandons it, it is still her child. We hesitate to confront wrongdoing within our own communities of faith because it feels like betraying family, yet silence slowly burns the very family we seek to protect. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom): A society that prays for honest leaders while applauding dishonest conduct should not be surprised when corruption becomes a regular guest at its table. Kenya’s Warning: When Obedience Replaces Faith Kenya’s Shakahola tragedy revealed what can happen when extreme religious claims, coercive influence and weak safeguards converge. By mid 2024 more than 440 bodies had been exhumed from the forest, victims associated with a movement whose leader stands accused of urging followers to starve themselves. It would be unjust to treat this as representative of Kenyan Christianity or of religion generally. Its enduring lesson is that no spiritual authority should ever stand beyond scrutiny, and no legitimate faith community should fear questions about money, safety or the treatment of its members. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom): The moment a spiritual leader demands the surrender of your conscience, your freedom or your safety, obedience may already have replaced faith. No Continent Holds A Monopoly On Hypocrisy Lest anyone imagine this is an African affliction, the record of the wider world is sobering. In 2021 an independent commission in France estimated that some 216,000 children had been sexually abused by Catholic clergy between 1950 and 2020, a figure that rose to about 330,000 when abuse by lay personnel associated with the Church was included. In the United States, investigations have exposed fraud, abuse and concealment across several religious organisations. The common thread is not any single creed but a familiar institutional instinct to protect reputation before victims, a temptation equally present in corporations and governments. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom): An institution that guards its image by hiding wrongdoing may preserve its reputation for a season while destroying the trust that gave it meaning. When The Offering Bowl Becomes A Laundry Perhaps the most troubling development is the tendency in some settings to equate material wealth with spiritual achievement, so that the man with the convoy is celebrated however the convoy was acquired while the honest teacher is quietly pitied. Legitimate prosperity and generous giving are no vice, and many successful entrepreneurs are models of integrity. The danger arises when wealth purchases admiration without explanation. A person who steals public resources and donates a fraction to charity has not converted plunder into piety, a generous donation is no substitute for restitution, and no religious title should serve as a diplomatic passport against criminal investigation. As the old saying goes, one falsehood spoils a thousand truths, and one stolen cedi placed in the offering bowl does not become holy simply because it was dropped there with a smile. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom): When unexplained wealth earns public applause and honest poverty attracts ridicule, a society has mistaken financial success for moral achievement. The Gospel Of Me, Myself And I When faith becomes chiefly a means of acquiring status, influence or personal advantage, the guiding question quietly shifts from how I can serve to what I can receive, so that compassion becomes conditional, generosity becomes publicity and leadership becomes entitlement. This is a betrayal of the traditions themselves. Christianity commands love of neighbour, Islam establishes zakat as an obligation to the poor, Judaism teaches tzedakah as justice rather than charity, Hinduism honours selfless service, Buddhism places compassion at the heart of the path, and African philosophies remind us that a person is a person through other people and owes duties to ancestors and generations yet unborn. Every one of them points outward, yet too many of us have turned them inward. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom): When the pursuit of personal blessing outgrows our concern for another person’s suffering, spirituality risks becoming selfishness dressed in sacred clothing. Rebuilding The Compass Together Renewal must begin within religious institutions themselves. Large ministries that handle substantial public donations should publish independently audited accounts, adopt safeguarding policies that protect children and vulnerable adults, and refer allegations of abuse or fraud to competent authorities rather than settling them behind closed doors. Interfaith councils can lead by agreeing common codes of conduct, showing that accountability is a shared virtue rather than an attack on any denomination. Governments, for their part, must protect freedom of worship scrupulously while enforcing laws against fraud, exploitation and violence without fear, favour or discrimination. The deeper shift, however, is one of mindset. Families and schools should teach ethical reasoning, financial literacy and the courage to ask respectful questions, so that young people understand that scrutiny is not disrespect. Congregations should celebrate service, honesty and responsibly earned success rather than extravagance. And citizens, believers and non believers alike, must recognise that integrity is the common ground on which all of us can stand, refusing to excuse misconduct simply because the alleged perpetrator shares our faith, our tribe or our political colours. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom): True faith strengthens conscience rather than silencing it, and genuine leadership welcomes accountability because integrity has nothing to fear from honest examination. Credit Where It Is Due None of this diminishes the extraordinary contribution of faith communities to human progress. Across Africa, churches, mosques and faith based organisations run schools, hospitals and relief programmes that serve millions, and countless leaders owe their education to mission institutions built by people who expected nothing in return. Those good works deserve gratitude, but they cannot be used as a blanket to cover wrongdoing elsewhere. The question is not whether religion should leave public life, but whether its professors will live its values. The Ledger We Will All Face One day the grand buildings, impressive titles, expensive vehicles and thunderous applause will belong to yesterday. The question history will ask is not how many people admired our religious appearance, but how many lives our conduct improved, how many vulnerable people we protected and whether our children inherited a society in which character mattered more than performance. Perhaps our greatest moral crisis is not that we have stopped believing, but that some of us have become remarkably skilled at professing beliefs we are unwilling to practise. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom): When faith becomes a shield for greed, deception and cruelty, it is not the sacred that has failed humanity; it is humanity that has abandoned the responsibilities it claims to hold sacred. A society does not become morally upright merely because its people worship frequently. It becomes morally stronger when justice, compassion, honesty and responsibility guide what they do after the final hymn has been sung and the last prayer has been said. Until then, each of us must look into the mirror and ask the question that refuses to go away. WHAT IS WRONG WITH US? ABOUT THE AUTHOR Ing. Professor Douglas Boateng is a pioneering international industrial, manufacturing and production systems engineer, governance strategist and Pan-African thought leader whose work continues to influence boardroom thinking, supply chain transformation and industrialisation strategy across the continent and beyond. As Africa’s first appointed Professor Extraordinaire in Supply Chain Management, he has long championed the integration of procurement, value chain development, industrialisation and governance into national and continental development agendas. An International Chartered Director and Chartered Engineer, he has received numerous lifetime achievement awards and authored several authoritative books. He is the scribe of the globally acclaimed NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom). His work rests on the conviction that Africa’s transformation — and the protection of its children — will come through deliberate action, strong institutions and leaders willing to build for generations they will never meet. © 2026 Ing. Prof. Douglas K. Boateng. All rights reserved.

items.title: Ghana’s mineral wealth: From extraction to local refining. The 2030 ambition
items.description: The manganese mine at Nsuta, in Ghana’s Western Region, has been shipping ore since 1916. More than a century later, the rock still leaves the country the way it comes out of the ground: raw, in bulk, bound for someone else’s furnaces. President John Mahama wants that to stop. “I say in 2030 there will be no mineral ore leaving Ghana,” he said in February. “We are not going to ship manganese ore, bauxite, iron ore out of Ghana raw. You must process all that locally.” It is a popular promise in a country that has long complained about selling cheap and buying dear. But the numbers show how far Ghana has to go. Right now, it refines about a third of the small-scale gold it sells abroad. It refines no manganese and no bauxite at all. The stakes are highest for gold. Between January and October, Ghana exported $30.4 billion of goods, and $20.9 billion of that was gold, Bank of Ghana data show. But most of it leaves as doré, a rough bar of mixed metals, and is purified to 99.99% in Dubai or Switzerland. The refining fees, the jobs and the know-how stay there. The government has now put dates and money behind the pledge. In the 2027 budget, presented on Nov. 12, Finance Minister Cassiel Ato Forson set aside $1.5 billion for mineral processing. At least 70% of gold from small-scale miners must be refined in Ghana by December 2027, and all of it by December 2028, when exports of raw small-scale gold will be banned. Half the country’s manganese and bauxite is to be processed locally by 2028, and all of it by 2030. The money is meant for a round-the-clock processing zone in the Western Region, a railway from Takoradi to the Nyinahin bauxite fields, a bigger Takoradi port and an inland port at Hamile, near the border with Burkina Faso. Gold is nearest the finish line. Small-scale miners, who in 2025 produced more of Ghana’s gold than the big corporate mines for the first time in over a century, turn out about 2.4 million ounces a year on average, according to the Ghana Chamber of Mines. That’s about 75 tonnes. The Ghana Gold Board, the state buyer says roughly 25 tonnes was refined locally between January and Oct. 20. In October alone, the share hit 94.6%. Ghana already has the refineries. Gold Coast Refinery and Royal Ghana Gold Refinery can together handle more than the small-scale sector produces. What the country lacks is trust. Gold bars move easily around the world only if they come from a refiner on the London Bullion Market Association’s “Good Delivery” list. No Ghanaian refiner is on it. In all of Africa, only South Africa’s Rand Refinery is. So when a Ghanaian bar lands in Dubai, where most of the country’s small-scale gold is sold, the buyer can test it again, melt it again or knock money off the price. Ghana pays about $13.80 an ounce to refine at home and can end up paying twice. Buyers also want to know where the gold came from. Illegal mining, known locally as galamsey, has poisoned rivers and torn up farmland, and Ghana currently has no traceability system that tracks small-scale gold from pit to bar. GoldBod is running a pilot covering 600 mines. Then there is smuggling. A refinery can only process the gold that reaches it, and the Chamber of Mines admits there are no official records of how much small-scale gold is mined. It counts what licensed buyers purchase instead. There is history, too. Gold Coast Refinery opened in 2016 to similar fanfare, then refined almost nothing for eight years after a change of government. Today’s flow of gold rests on agreements a future government could tear up. Manganese and bauxite are a different story. For this sector, Ghana is starting from zero. Ghana Manganese Company, the country’s only manganese miner, has long shipped its ore to its parent company’s plants in China, according to the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources. The ore leaves at about 27% manganese. A $450 million refinery to upgrade it was announced in 2024. It hasn’t been built, and nobody has said how much it could process. Bauxite is the stranger case. Ghana mines it at Awaso, and it also owns an aluminium smelter, the Volta Aluminium Company, or VALCO, in Tema. The two have never been connected. Bauxite must be turned into a white powder called alumina before it can become aluminium, and Ghana has no plant that does that. So all its bauxite is shipped out raw, and VALCO imports all the alumina it uses, according to GIADEC, the state aluminium company. Ghana sells the ingredient and buys it back half-made. Ghana Bauxite Company has plans for an alumina refinery that would make 500,000 tonnes a year at first and up to 1.5 million later. It is still being studied. If we line the numbers up the size of the job becomes plain. For gold, Ghana needs to add about 27 tonnes of refining by the end of 2027 and another 22 tonnes a year later, roughly 1.4 tonnes a week. The gap may be a little smaller than it looks, since the 25-tonne figure covers less than 10 months. For manganese and bauxite, every tonne of capacity still has to be built. Even that may understate the task. Output is rising faster than the averages suggest. Ghana mined 5.2 million tonnes of manganese and about 2 million tonnes of bauxite in 2025, and plants sized to the past would leave plenty of ore with nowhere to go. The government hasn’t published a forecast of how much it expects to mine in 2030, so nobody can say exactly how big the new plants need to be. Ghana has opened refineries with speeches before and watched them sit idle. This time there is a date, a budget line and a president who keeps repeating the pledge abroad. Whether that’s enough will be measured in tonnes after the deadlines.

items.title: Ga Mantse urges newly called Ga-Dangme lawyers to defend Ga-Dangme heritage and reshape its narrative
items.description: The Ga Mantse, King Tackie Teiko Tsuru II, has urged newly called lawyers of Ga-Dangme descent to use their professional expertise to protect the interests, heritage and dignity of the Ga State. He has also challenged the young legal practitioners to take an active interest in issues affecting the Ga people and contribute meaningfully to the development and preservation of their traditional institutions. The Ga Mantse made the call when a delegation of newly called Ga-Dangme lawyers, led by Samuel Adjei Adjetey, Esther Naa Dodua Ribeiro, Oliver Nii Adjabeng Quarcoo, Samuel Adjetey Adjei and Raymond Nii Doodo Larbie, paid a courtesy visit to the Ga Palace. The visit was to formally introduce themselves to the traditional ruler and reaffirm their commitment to serving the Ga State through their legal training, expertise and professional experience. Addressing the delegation, HRM King Tackie Teiko Tsuru II emphasised the important role lawyers can play in shaping public discourse, protecting institutional interests and ensuring that the history and identity of the Ga people are properly represented. He urged the newly qualified lawyers to become active participants in efforts to reshape the narrative surrounding the Ga State, stressing the need for them to use their professional standing to promote the truth about the Ga people and safeguard their collective heritage. The Ga Mantse further encouraged the lawyers to consider making their services available to the Ga Traditional Council Judicial Committee and form an alliance of Lawyers in Defence of the Ga State to strengthen efforts aimed at protecting the traditional state’s legal interests, heritage and institutional integrity. He noted that the involvement of legal professionals with strong connections to the Ga State would enhance its capacity to address legal matters, defend its interests and preserve the dignity of its traditional institutions. The King also urged the younger generation of Ga-Dangme professionals not to regard their professional achievements merely as personal milestones but as an opportunity to give back to their roots and contribute to the progress of their community. In their response, the newly called lawyers expressed appreciation to the Ga Mantse for receiving them and acknowledged his efforts towards changing what they described as the negative narrative surrounding the Ga State and Ga-Dangme people. They commended King Tackie Teiko Tsuru II for his leadership and initiatives aimed at restoring the image, dignity and recognition of the Ga people. The lawyers reaffirmed their willingness to make their legal knowledge and professional competencies available to support the Ga State, particularly in matters concerning its development, traditional institutions, cultural heritage and legal interests. They also described the engagement as an important opportunity to strengthen their relationship with the Ga Palace and identify practical ways of contributing to the development of the Ga-Dangme community. The visit underscores the importance of professional involvement in traditional governance and the role of indigenous professionals in safeguarding the identity, heritage and interests of their communities. It also presents an opportunity for the Ga State to harness the expertise of a new generation of legal practitioners to strengthen its institutions and ensure that its interests are adequately represented.

items.title: Violences à Siguiri : 69 interpellations, 46 personnes écrouées (Procureur)
items.description: La justice affiche sa fermeté après les récents troubles à l’ordre public survenus à Siguiri. Selon Marouane Baldé, le procureur général près la Cour d’appel de Kankan, 69 personnes ont été interpellées par les forces de défense et de sécurité. Parmi elles, 46 ont été déférées devant le parquet du tribunal de première instance de Siguiri et placées sous mandat de dépôt. En mission dans la préfecture, le procureur général a dressé un premier bilan judiciaire des procédures engagées à la suite des événements qui ont secoué la localité. Les faits reprochés aux personnes interpellées portent notamment sur des violences, la participation à des manifestations non autorisées, des agressions contre les dépositaires de la force publique ainsi que des atteintes aux symboles de l’État. « À l’occasion de ces différentes manifestations, 69 personnes ont été interpellées par les forces de défense et de sécurité. 46 sont déjà déférées devant le parquet d’instance de Siguiri et placées sous mandat de dépôt », a précisé le magistrat. Dix mineurs présentés devant le juge des enfants La situation des mineurs impliqués dans ces événements fait également l’objet d’un suivi judiciaire particulier. Le procureur général a indiqué que dix mineurs ont déjà été présentés devant le juge des enfants, tandis que d’autres procédures les concernant étaient encore en cours. Face à la gravité des faits évoqués, le chef du parquet général a affiché une ligne de fermeté. Il a assuré que les personnes reconnues coupables des infractions poursuivies devront répondre de leurs actes devant les juridictions compétentes. « Il y a eu des violences, des participations à des troubles sans autorisation, des faits de violence à l’égard des dépositaires de la force publique, des forces de défense et de sécurité, des symboles de l’État atteints. Ces faits ne resteront pas impunis », a-t-il averti. Le procureur général a enfin réaffirmé qu’aucune violation de la loi pénale ne serait tolérée dans le ressort de la Cour d’appel de Kankan. Un avertissement qui traduit la volonté du parquet de faire respecter l’ordre public et les institutions de la République.

items.title: Gunmen behead, burn 60-year-old man in Cross River
items.description: By Ike Uchechukwu, Calabar Gunmen have killed a 60-year-old man, James Edi Diwa, and set his body and motorcycle ablaze in Boki Local Government Area of Cross River State. The incident reportedly occurred at about 5:20pm along the Isobendeghe–Boje Road, where Diwa, a native of Katchuan in Irruan community, was riding his motorcycle when he was ambushed. The attackers allegedly shot him, beheaded him and set his remains and motorcycle on fire. The Cross River State Police Command disclosed this in a statement on Thursday by its Police Public Relations Officer, ASP Eitokpah Sunday. According to the police, the deceased’s wife, Mrs Schola Abang, reported the incident at the Boki Divisional Police Headquarters on November 13, 2026, at about 6:10am. The statement said police operatives visited the scene following the report and commenced preliminary investigations. “The Cross River State Police Command has commenced an investigation into the gruesome murder of a 60-year-old man, identified as James Edi Diwa, who was allegedly ambushed and killed by unidentified gunmen along the Isobendeghe–Boje Road in Boki Local Government Area,” the statement said. The Commissioner of Police, Mr Ajo Geoffrey Ordue, condemned the killing and directed relevant operational and investigative units to intensify efforts to identify and arrest those responsible. The command said no arrest had been made as of the time the statement was issued. Ordue assured residents that the police would work to bring the perpetrators to justice. He urged members of the public to remain calm, refrain from taking the law into their hands and provide credible information that could assist the investigation. The post Gunmen behead, burn 60-year-old man in Cross River appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Housing Minister calls for dedicated housing bank to tackle Ghana’s widening housing deficit
items.description: The Minister for Works, Housing and Water Resources, Ahmed Ibrahim, has called for the establishment of a dedicated housing development bank to improve access to long-term financing for real estate developers and accelerate housing delivery in Ghana. He says the absence of affordable and sustainable financing remains one of the major constraints facing the country’s real estate sector, warning that government alone cannot bridge the widening housing deficit. Speaking at a sensitisation programme on the Borrowers and Lenders Act, 2020 (Act 1052), and the operations of the Bank of Ghana’s Collateral Registry for members of the Real Estate Agency Council in Accra, Mr Ibrahim urged the central bank to support the development of a specialised financial institution to finance housing projects. He cited the former Bank for Housing and Construction as an example of how specialised financing institutions could support large-scale housing development in the country. He also suggested that Republic Bank could be strengthened and adequately resourced to play a greater role in financing the housing sector. Mr Ibrahim said Ghana’s housing deficit, estimated at 1.8 million units in 2021, had since widened, making it necessary to attract more private capital into housing delivery. He argued that improving access to credit for developers, investors and prospective homeowners would be critical to expanding housing supply and addressing the country’s housing challenges. The minister commended the Bank of Ghana for its recent reduction in the monetary policy rate, describing the lower interest rate environment as an opportunity for increased investment in the real estate sector. He said the benefits of improved macroeconomic conditions should translate into more affordable financing, increased construction activity and ultimately lower housing costs. Mr Ibrahim further described the real estate sector as a major source of employment, noting that housing development creates opportunities for construction workers, artisans, engineers, architects, surveyors, brokers and other professionals. He said the sector could play a significant role in addressing youth unemployment if supported with the necessary financing and regulatory reforms. The sensitisation programme is aimed at deepening understanding of the Borrowers and Lenders Act, 2020 (Act 1052), and the operations of the Collateral Registry, particularly in relation to asset-based lending and access to credit. The minister said effective implementation of the legal framework would improve transparency in lending transactions, reduce lending risks and enable individuals and businesses to use a wider range of assets as collateral. He called for stronger collaboration between government, financial institutions, regulators and real estate practitioners to create an investor-friendly housing market and accelerate private-sector participation.

items.title: Bolt steps up ride-hailing safety education in Ghana ahead of festive season
items.description: Ride-hailing company Bolt has intensified its safety education campaign in Ghana, highlighting driver vetting, passenger verification and shared responsibility between drivers and passengers. The company outlined its prevention-first approach at a Safety Experience Workshop in Accra on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. The event brought together representatives of the National Road Safety Authority (NRSA), passengers, driver-partners and the media. Bolt said its safety measures begin before a driver accepts a trip, with identity verification and checks on driver and vehicle documentation forming part of the onboarding process. Passengers are also encouraged to take precautions before entering a vehicle by checking the driver and vehicle details displayed on the app to ensure they match the information provided for their trip. Other in-app safeguards include Pickup Codes, which help passengers confirm they are entering the correct vehicle, and voluntary Rider Verification. Jonathan Ahumah-Sackey, Senior Operations Manager at Bolt Ghana, said the company believes safety should be addressed before incidents occur. “Safety should not begin when something goes wrong. It starts with the checks we put in place before a driver accepts a trip, the information passengers receive before entering a vehicle and the safeguards available throughout the journey,” he said. The campaign comes as Bolt prepares to strengthen safety awareness ahead of the festive season, a period when travel and social activities typically increase. The company also cited findings from its 2025 Ipsos Safety Index, which indicated that 81% of surveyed ride-hailing users in Ghana considered ride-hailing safer than other transport options. The workshop forms part of Bolt’s efforts to familiarise users with available safety features and encourage drivers and passengers to take an active role in making journeys safer.

items.title: Aucune consigne d’exemption des infractions routières des voitures de l’État
items.description: Aucune note de la Présidence du gouvernement n’a été émise pour empêcher la verbalisation des véhicules de l’État en mission officielle. Un responsable au sein de la Chefferie de l'Exécutif a démenti auprès de Hespress les informations relayées sur les réseaux sociaux, mettant fin aux spéculations autour d’un prétendu dispositif d’exemption. La source d'Hespress a ainsi démenti l’existence d’une note ou d’une circulaire émanant des services de la présidence du gouvernement invitant les autorités compétentes à ne pas enregistrer les infractions commises par les véhicules administratifs en déplacement pour les besoins de service. Les publications relayées ces derniers jours affirmaient qu’une instruction aurait été adressée dans ce sens, soulevant plusieurs interrogations sur les administrations concernées, les modalités permettant de justifier le caractère officiel d’une mission et les limites d’une éventuelle exemption. Ces informations ont suscité des réactions contrastées. Certains internautes ont estimé qu’un traitement particulier pouvait se justifier pour faciliter les interventions urgentes ou certaines missions administratives. D’autres ont, au contraire, insisté sur la nécessité d’appliquer le Code de la route à tous les usagers, sans distinction, et de renforcer le contrôle de l’utilisation des véhicules de l’État, notamment en dehors des horaires de travail. The post Aucune consigne d’exemption des infractions routières des voitures de l’État appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Gender Minister calls for stronger coordination to end violence against children
items.description: The Minister for Gender, Children and Social Protection, Dr Agnes Naa Momo Lartey, has called for stronger coordination among government institutions, families, schools and communities to strengthen efforts to prevent and respond to violence against children. She said ending violence against children required more than individual interventions, stressing the need for effective child protection systems that respond to the needs of children. Speaking at the Second Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children in Manila, Philippines, Dr Lartey said parental and caregiver support, safe schools and effective response systems must work together to ensure children receive the protection they need. She made the remarks during a session on “Strengthening Child Protection Systems: A Multi-Sectoral Approach to Prevention and Responses – Scaling Prevention of Violence Against Children through the 3 Breakthroughs”. The Minister stressed that when children report abuse or violence, functional systems must be available to respond promptly and provide the necessary support. Highlighting Ghana’s progress, she said the Integrated Social Services initiative now covers all 261 districts, bringing together social welfare, health, education, justice and social protection actors to improve case management and referrals. She also cited the training of 5,375 social workers, police officers and judicial personnel, alongside efforts to strengthen child protection legislation and professionalise the social service workforce. On interventions to support families and communities, Dr Lartey highlighted the National Parenting Strategy and prevention campaigns that have reached more than 3.5 million people. She further noted that every public senior high school now has trained Safe Space Focal Persons to strengthen child protection, while efforts are underway to link school reporting mechanisms directly to district social welfare services. Despite the progress, the Minister acknowledged challenges, including workforce shortages, dependence on development partner funding and fragmented data systems. She called for increased domestic investment, stronger accountability and improved coordination to ensure the sustainability and quality of child protection services. Drawing lessons from Ghana’s experience, Dr Lartey identified three priorities: coordinating services around the needs of children rather than individual institutions, strengthening existing government systems, and investing simultaneously in the social service workforce and data systems. She emphasised that protecting children was a collective responsibility that required sustained action to ensure prevention efforts translated into lasting improvements in their safety and well-being.

items.title: FCC sets aside high court rulings upholding infrastructure cess in Sindh, KP
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) on Thursday set aside high court rulings upholding the infrastructure cess imposed by the Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa governments. The case pertained to the Sindh Development and Maintenance of Infrastructure Cess Act, 2017 and the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Infrastructure Development Cess Act, 2022, including amendments introduced through the KP Finance Act, 2024. Headed by FCC Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan, a two-judge bench, also comprising Justice Aamer Farooq, had taken up a batch of 568 petitions by private petitioners challenging decisions by the Sindh High Court (SHC) and the Peshawar High Court (PHC) upholding the cesses. The FCC bench examined the constitutional limits of provincial taxation in relation to imports, exports, customs-related transactions and the movement of goods across provincial boundaries. The Sindh infrastructure cess controversy originated in 1994 and was subsequently governed by the Sindh Development and Maintenance of Infrastructure Cess Act, 2017, which provided for taxes on goods entering or leaving Sindh from or for outside the country through air or sea. On June 4, 2021, the SHC upheld the levy. Similarly, the KP Infrastructure Development Cess Act, 2022, imposed cess on the transportation and movement of goods in the province. Section 14 of the KP Finance Act, 2024, amended Section 3 of the 2022 Act to enhance the cess rate from one to two per cent. The PHC, through its Nov 14, 2025 judgement, dismissed 157 petitions challenging the levy and upheld its legality. The judgements of both high courts were subsequently challenged before the FCC. The petitioners argued that the provinces lacked constitutional authority to impose fiscal levies on imports, exports and goods falling within the federal legislative domain. They maintained that the impugned laws encroached upon Parliament’s exclusive legislative competence. Consequently, the provincial provisions and the high court judgements upholding them could not be sustained. Senior counsel Hafiz Ehsaan Ahmad Khokhar, while representing the secretary of the Revenue Division and the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), submitted that the impugned provincial levies had to be examined in the light of Articles 141 and 142(a) of the Constitution, read with Entries 27, 43 and 59 of Part I of the Federal Legislative List (FLL) in the Fourth Schedule. He explained that Entry 27 covered imports and exports across customs frontiers, inter-provincial trade and commerce and trade with foreign countries, whereas Entry 43 specifically assigned customs duties, including export duties, to the federation. The counsel contended that under Article 142(a), Parliament had exclusive legislative competence over matters enumerated in the FLL. The constitutional character of a levy, he argued, must be determined by its true nature, taxable event, fiscal incidence, charging provisions and actual operation, not merely by its nomenclature as an infrastructure cess. A provincial levy imposing an additional fiscal burden on imported or exported goods and operating through the customs-clearance mechanism directly engaged the federal legislative domain, he said. He also referred to Article 163, explaining that the provincial power to impose taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments could not be extended to customs duties or other subjects constitutionally assigned to the Parliament. The counsel further argued that a provincial legislature could not acquire legislative competence over a federal subject merely by describing a customs-linked fiscal levy as an infrastructure cess. Meanwhile, the Sindh and KP governments defended their respective laws, arguing that the taxes were provincial levies intended to finance infrastructure development and road facilities. They maintained that it was not a customs or export duty and that the provincial assemblies were competent to legislate on such matters under Article 142(c) of the Constitution and the impugned judgements were legal. The additional attorney general supported the federation’s position, submitting that the provincial governments lacked legislative competence to impose levies falling within the FLL. After hearing the arguments, the FCC set aside the two high court judgements and declared that the legislations were beyond the legislative competence of the provinces.

items.title: Etat civil : L’ANEC à l’écoute des réalités de Kédougou
items.description: Malgré une hausse des déclarations de naissances, de mariages et de décès entre 2023 et 2025, la région de Kédougou reste en dessous de la moyenne nationale en matière d’état civil. Ce constat a été fait lors d’un comité régional de développement (CRD) organisé par l’Agence nationale de l’état civil (ANEC), en prélude aux concertations nationales de décembre. Présidant la rencontre, l’adjoint au gouverneur chargé du développement, Mouhamadoul Moustapha Gaye, a souligné les difficultés liées à l’éloignement des villages, à la faiblesse de la couverture internet et à la conservation des archives. Il a appelé à des solutions adaptées aux réalités locales. Parmi les pistes évoquées figurent la création de centres secondaires d’état civil, la digitalisation des services, notamment grâce à la connexion satellitaire Starlink, ainsi que le renforcement des capacités des agents. A lire aussi : Kédougou :La boutique de droit en quête de pérennisation Pour le directeur général de l’ANEC, Matar Ndao, ces consultations permettent de recueillir les préoccupations des acteurs locaux afin de mieux orienter les décisions nationales. Les échanges ont également porté sur la reconstitution des archives détériorées et la professionnalisation des agents. Au terme de la rencontre, l’autorité administrative a plaidé pour un renforcement du dialogue entre l’ANEC et les collectivités territoriales, afin de faciliter l’accès des populations à leurs droits fondamentaux. Amadou DIOP (Correspondant)

items.title: Paris Padel Maroc lance un circuit de huit rendez-vous entre la France et le Maroc
items.description: De Paris à Marrakech, Rabat et Casablanca, Paris Padel Maroc veut faire du padel bien plus qu’un simple sport. L’association lance un circuit de huit rendez-vous entre décembre 2026 et juillet 2027, mêlant compétition, convivialité et networking entre les deux rives de la Méditerranée. Le padel devient progressivement un nouvel espace de rencontre entre la France et le Maroc. Forte de 12 éditions et de plus de 2 000 joueurs réunis depuis sa création, l’association Paris Padel Maroc (PPM) franchit une nouvelle étape en lançant un circuit régulier de huit rendez-vous entre Paris et plusieurs villes marocaines. De décembre 2026 à juillet 2027, le programme proposera quatre étapes à Paris, au 4Padel Boulogne, et quatre temps forts au Maroc, notamment à Marrakech, Rabat et Casablanca. L’ambition : faire du terrain de padel un lieu où se croisent sportifs, entrepreneurs, cadres, étudiants et professionnels. Le développement de ce circuit intervient alors que le padel connaît une croissance importante à l’échelle internationale. La discipline compte désormais environ 40 millions de pratiquants dans le monde et la France a franchi le cap des 5 000 terrains, selon le World Padel Report 2026 de la Fédération internationale de padel (FIP). Au Maroc, le développement est également marqué. Le nombre de terrains serait passé de 96 à 200 en deux ans, tandis que les tournois féminins seraient passés de 23 à 95, selon les données de la Fédération royale marocaine de tennis. Mais pour Paris Padel Maroc, l’intérêt de la discipline ne se résume pas à ces chiffres. Le sport constitue également un moyen de créer des liens. « Quand on est entrepreneur, on enchaîne les salons et les conférences, où l’on échange des cartes de visite. Sur un court de padel, tout change : on joue à quatre, on rit, on se parle avant, pendant et après le match, et on rencontre des personnes qu’on ne croiserait pas ailleurs » , explique Ali Lefriyekh, entrepreneur et cofondateur de Paris Padel Maroc. Du tournoi ponctuel à un véritable circuit Créée à Paris en avril 2025 à la suite d’un premier tournoi, l’association a rapidement fait du rapprochement entre la France et le Maroc son principal axe de développement. En un an et demi, PPM a organisé 12 éditions et réuni plus de 2 000 joueurs. En juillet dernier, son Padel Summer Festival organisé à Casablanca avait notamment proposé 164 matchs en trois jours. L’association avait également profité de la Coupe du monde 2026 pour installer une fan zone marocaine au Grand Rex à Paris. Forte de cette dynamique, Paris Padel Maroc entend désormais passer d’une succession de tournois à un calendrier régulier entre les deux pays. À Paris, le circuit sera porté par Chaabi Bank, devenue en octobre partenaire titre des rendez-vous organisés au 4Padel Boulogne, désormais baptisés Chaabi Bank Padel Series. Un circuit ouvert à tous les niveaux L’organisation veut également éviter de réserver ses événements aux seuls joueurs expérimentés. Chaque rendez-vous sera accessible à différents niveaux, avec notamment une catégorie dédiée aux débutants, baptisée Rise, ainsi que des tableaux Bronze, Silver, Gold et Platinum. Des compétitions 100 % féminines seront également proposées à chaque édition. À partir du 12 décembre, certaines catégories seront en outre homologuées par la Fédération française de tennis (FFT). Le format associera compétition et animations : matchs en paires, phases de poules et finales, remise des trophées, retransmission des résultats sur écran géant, matchs d’exhibition avec des joueurs professionnels et animations hors terrain. Chaque participant recevra également un maillot officiel, tandis que les rencontres seront prolongées par des moments de convivialité et de networking. Huit rendez-vous entre Paris et le Maroc Le calendrier débutera le 12 décembre 2026 à Paris, avec la première Chaabi Bank Padel Series au 4Padel Boulogne. Le circuit se poursuivra quelques jours plus tard au Maroc, avec la Padel Winter Party, programmée les 26 et 27 décembre à Marrakech, au MĀRA Padel Club. Quatre autres étapes parisiennes sont prévues en février, avril et juin 2027, tandis que le Maroc accueillera plusieurs temps forts : un Gala Padel des stars en mars, une étape à Rabat le 15 mai, puis un rendez-vous à Casablanca le 17 juillet. À travers ce calendrier, Paris Padel Maroc souhaite installer un nouveau rendez-vous sportif et lifestyle entre la France et le Maroc, en misant sur un modèle qui associe sport, rencontres professionnelles et convivialité. L’association ambitionne ainsi de faire du padel un véritable trait d’union entre les deux pays, avec des événements réguliers capables de réunir aussi bien les passionnés de la discipline que ceux qui souhaitent simplement découvrir cet univers. Le padel devient ainsi le prétexte à la rencontre, tandis que la création de liens entre les communautés française et marocaine constitue le véritable fil conducteur du circuit. The post Paris Padel Maroc lance un circuit de huit rendez-vous entre la France et le Maroc appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: British Entrepreneur Rio Kavanagh targets financing and quality gaps in Ghana’s agricultural exports
items.description: An Accra liaison desk will coordinate suppliers, portside storage and European buyers, with a target of moving 500 metric tonnes through Tema by June 2027. Finding an overseas buyer does not always settle the hardest part of an agricultural export deal. A supplier still has to assemble the goods, preserve their quality and cover the interval before payment arrives. Rio Kavanagh is building his Ghana operation around that stretch of the trade. The British entrepreneur has opened an Accra liaison desk through his UK company, Rio Kavanagh Holdings Ltd, to coordinate exports of processed cocoa derivatives, raw cashew nuts and shea produce. The operation links licensed aggregators in the Ashanti, Bono and Northern regions with food and industrial buyers in the UK and Europe, using Tema Port as its shipping gateway. Kavanagh said his assessment of West African supply chains over the past year repeatedly brought him back to two problems: working capital tied up between collection and export, and quality disputes that can reduce the value of a consignment. “First, mid-sized Ghanaian aggregators have no trouble finding international buyers, but high domestic cedi borrowing rates and long settlement delays tie up their working capital between farmgate collection and export,” he said. “Second, inconsistent grading and moisture levels often lead to costly price deductions or rejections once cargo reaches Tema Port.” The desk, opened in November, brings supplier liaison, pre-shipment checks and export scheduling into a local operation. Kavanagh’s strategy and risk team remains in the UK. “I wanted a physical base on the ground in Ghana rather than trying to coordinate West African trade from Yorkshire,” he said. Connecting stock with settlement The business is entering an export sector that has been growing. The Ghana Export Promotion Authority’s 2025 report puts non-traditional export earnings at about US$5.01 billion, up 30.7 per cent from 2024, with cocoa derivatives driving much of the increase. Kavanagh’s approach is to arrange the buyer, quality checks and storage around the same consignment. Before opening the desk, the company put in place a trade-facilitation arrangement designed to handle more than £2.2 million in annualised cross-border trade across its three commodity categories. The figure describes the value of trade the arrangement is structured to support. Its components include insured portside storage, pre-shipment quality compliance and forward buyer settlement. “We do not operate as a bank or traditional lender; we act as a trade-coordination and risk-management desk,” Kavanagh said. By matching verified stock with buyers arranged in advance, the company aims to shorten the wait for suppliers to receive payment and reduce their reliance on domestic borrowing. Quality verification is central to that process: the goods being prepared for shipment must meet the requirements of the buyer already lined up to take them. Storage and staff on the ground The infrastructure spending has gone into capacity within existing licensed warehouses near Tema and moisture-testing and grading equipment for local logistics partners. The company has also leased its Accra office. “We deliberately avoided spending capital building new warehouses when good certified facilities already exist around Tema Port,” Kavanagh said. Four people currently work on the ground, covering supplier liaison, quality inspection and port scheduling. As export batches increase, the company plans to recruit a further six to eight local staff for field quality assurance, warehouse receipt auditing and export compliance. The recruitment effort is aimed at Ghanaian agricultural logistics graduates and experienced port specialists, with training in European buyer grading standards and forward-contract risk management. These roles will support the work between collection, storage and shipment, where the desk is concentrating its resources. Supplier onboarding is complete, and pre-shipment quality and moisture-grading checks are under way along the Tema corridor, Kavanagh said. The next stage is to clear the first 500 metric tonnes of verified produce through the port in the first half of 2027. The company then aims to reach an annualised trade volume of £2.2 million by the end of that year.

items.title: Newmont tops Ghana Club 100 as President Mahama urges businesses to tap into $10bn New Economy programme
items.description: President John Mahama has urged Ghanaian businesses to position themselves to benefit from the government’s US$10 billion New Economy Programme, which seeks to transform the economy through investments in eight strategic sectors. The programme targets sectors including agriculture, agribusiness, irrigation, textiles and garments as part of efforts to expand Ghana’s productive capacity and accelerate industrial growth. Speaking at the 22nd Ghana Club 100 Awards in Accra on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, President Mahama called on businesses to take advantage of the opportunities the programme presents to expand their operations and contribute to national development. He also commended the Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, Elizabeth Ofosu-Adjare, for her commitment to industrialisation, factory development and efforts to expand Ghana’s industrial base. The awards ceremony was organised by the Ghana Investment Promotion Centre (GIPC) in collaboration with the Ministry of Trade, Agribusiness and Industry. President Mahama reaffirmed the government’s commitment to maintaining macroeconomic stability, improving access to credit and implementing business-friendly reforms to support private sector growth. He, however, called for urgent interventions by the Ministries of Trade and Transport and other relevant stakeholders to address port congestion and regulatory bottlenecks affecting businesses. Newmont emerged as the overall winner of the 22nd Ghana Club 100 Awards, taking the top position among the country’s 100 best-performing companies. President Mahama congratulated Newmont and the other award recipients, urging them to continue expanding their businesses and contributing to Ghana’s economic growth. For her part, Ms Ofosu-Adjare urged the award-winning companies to embrace the “One More Ghana” initiative to drive industrial growth, create jobs and expand the country’s exports.

items.title: Rice quality must match production levels in Ghana’s self-sufficiency drive – Trade Minister
items.description: The Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, Elizabeth Ofosu-Adjare, has called on players in Ghana’s rice value chain to prioritise quality alongside increased production as the country intensifies efforts to achieve rice self-sufficiency. She said boosting local rice production must go hand in hand with improved quality standards, modern processing technology and stronger collaboration among industry stakeholders. Speaking at an introductory engagement with players in the rice value chain on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, the Minister called for a coordinated approach involving farmers, processors, millers, traders and other industry players to develop practical policies that address the sector’s needs and productive capacity. She reaffirmed the government’s commitment to creating a sustainable market for locally produced rice, disclosing that one of its immediate priorities was to ensure that public institutions, including schools, hospitals and prisons, sourced their rice requirements from local producers. On quality assurance, Ms Ofosu-Adjare urged farmers and processors to invest in modern equipment such as colour sorters, destoners and graders to improve the quality, appearance and competitiveness of locally produced rice. She noted that Ghanaian consumers were becoming increasingly particular about the quality of rice they purchased, stressing the need for local producers to meet consumer expectations and build confidence in the Ghanaian rice brand. The President of the Ghana Rice Inter-Professional Body (GRIB), Nana Adjei Ayeh II, who led the delegation, welcomed the government’s decision to strengthen collaboration with stakeholders in the rice industry. He also called for support to address the activities of charlatans within the rice production value chain.

items.title: Renforcement des relations maroco-sénégalaises : les universités Ibn Zohr et Cheikh Ahmadoul Khadim misent sur la recherche scientifique
items.description: Les universités Ibn Zohr du Maroc et Cheikh Ahmadoul Khadim (UCAK) de Touba entendent faire de la recherche scientifique un levier de consolidation des relations entre le Sénégal et le Maroc. Dans cette perspective, une délégation de l'université Ibn Zohr séjourne à Touba, du 18 au 21 novembre 2026, autour du thème : « La recherche scientifique et son rôle dans le renforcement des relations maroco-sénégalaises ». Cette visite s'inscrit dans le cadre de la mise en œuvre du partenariat entre les deux établissements universitaires. Elle constitue une occasion de renforcer leur coopération scientifique et de jeter les bases de nouvelles perspectives de collaboration. Pour le recteur de l'UCAK, le professeur Lamine Guèye, le choix du thème revêt une importance particulière en raison de son caractère fédérateur. Il a salué l'initiative des responsables de l'université Ibn Zohr, qui ont choisi de concrétiser leur partenariat avec l'établissement de Touba à travers un programme axé sur la recherche scientifique. Selon lui, les échanges entre les deux délégations devraient déboucher sur des projets de recherche communs, susceptibles de contribuer au rapprochement des deux institutions, mais également au renforcement des relations entre le Sénégal et le Maroc. A lire aussi : Le Cercle Sénégal-Maroc d’amitié et de fraternité dévoile ses ambitions au khalife général des mourides Prenant la parole au nom de la délégation marocaine, le professeur El Bachir Abrazac a, pour sa part, insisté sur la vocation sociale de la recherche scientifique. À ses yeux, celle-ci ne prend véritablement tout son sens que lorsqu'elle permet d'apporter des réponses concrètes aux préoccupations des sociétés. Dans cette perspective, il estime que les travaux scientifiques doivent également contribuer à consolider les liens historiques et les relations d'amitié entre les peuples sénégalais et marocain. Il a, en outre, souligné l'importance des résultats de la recherche comme outils d'aide à la décision pour les autorités et les décideurs publics. Ces derniers, selon lui, doivent pouvoir s'appuyer sur les connaissances scientifiques avant d'engager leurs choix et leurs politiques. À travers cette rencontre, les deux universités ambitionnent ainsi de donner une nouvelle dimension à leur coopération, en faisant de la production et du partage des connaissances des instruments au service du rapprochement maroco-sénégalais. Birane DIOP, correspondant

items.title: Nana Ato Arthur questions whether soon to be assessed MMDCEs were told their targets at the start of the year
items.description: A former Head of the Local Government Service, Dr Nana Ato Arthur, has asked whether Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs) were told at the beginning of the year what indicators they would be measured by, as the President moves to have their performance assessed. Speaking on Adom FM’s Dwaso Nsem on Thursday, November 19, he reacted to the President’s directive for an assessment of MMDCEs. “The President’s directive is good, but were they told from the beginning of the year the indicators they were going to be measured by?” he asked. Dr Arthur said MMDCEs must have a say in the key performance indicators (KPIs) used to judge them, and that the targets should cover only what falls within their control. He explained that while he was in office, he held meetings with all regional ministers and their chief directors in November and December to sign performance contracts for the coming year. The same was done with MMDCEs and their coordinating directors. “We meet them because they must have control over what you’re going to assess them by. So when we’re determining the key performance areas and the key performance indicators, both sides must agree that ‘these are within our control, so it’s fair if you assess us by them’,” he said. At the Regional Coordinating Councils (RCCs), the chief director, representing the entire staff, signs with the regional minister; at the Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs), the coordinating director signs on behalf of the assembly’s staff, while the MMDCE signs as the head. Dr Arthur also stressed that funds should follow functions. “If you say you’re going to assess someone’s performance but the person didn’t get what he needed to get the work done, how do you assess his performance?” he asked.
