items.title: The Secretary of Imprecision
items.description: O ver the past several days , as anxious Americans watched software systems crash, air traffic halt, and banking services glitch—wondering each time whether the country was falling victim to a catastrophic cyberattack—it has been Markwayne Mullin’s job to reassure them. Delivering clear and careful explanations, unfortunately, is not his forte. The Department of Homeland Security secretary’s speaking style is more free-associative. Mullin first rose to prominence by building his family’s plumbing business into a home-services giant in northeast Oklahoma. His sentences still tend to travel like a drain line, making loops and turns en route to an unseen destination. He doesn’t seem to work from talking points. Mullin parlayed this folksy manner and Everyman relatability into a successful bid for Congress in 2012. He wore a cowboy hat around Washington, D.C., and became one of President Trump’s fiercest allies on Capitol Hill. When Trump picked him to replace Kristi Noem at DHS earlier this year, he carried a reputation as the martial artist of MAGA politics. This made Mullin a somewhat unusual choice for a job that, until Trump’s second term, had typically been held by more buttoned-up figures who choose their words carefully, especially during moments of crisis. Soon after the FAA lifted its hours-long ground stop on Friday evening, Mullin appeared alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and announced that the problem was likely caused by the FAA’s own upgrades. This put the onus on Duffy, who stared at the floor and shook his head. The two have not appeared at briefings together since. Three nights later, after thousands of Chase Bank customers were unable to access their accounts and other financial institutions’ clients reported problems with digital payments, Mullin appeared on Sean Hannity’s Fox News show and described a conversation that he’d had a few hours earlier with “one guy that’s very smart with tech” (but not, Mullin made clear, Elon Musk) who had claimed that AI was indirectly causing the outages. “As it starts self-fixing itself it’s like doing a change order on a house,” Mullin said, using a home-improvement analogy. It wasn’t clear whether this assessment was coming from cybersecurity experts—particularly those at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is under Mullin’s command at DHS. Mullin said with “98 percent certainty” that the outages were not cyberattacks. By Tuesday, Mullin was able to add that last 2 percent, saying during a CNBC interview: “I can tell you with complete certainty that we are not under attack.” He gave no indication of how he’d arrived at that view. (Three minutes later, his certainty regressed to 98 percent.) One frustrated senior DHS official who didn’t want to be identified bad-mouthing the boss told me that Mullin “gives the perception that he’s winging it,” adding that “he’s giving Biden a run for his money with the frequency of gaffes.” [ Read: The secretary of homeland ] Late-night comedians are now mocking him—along with right-wing commentators. The podcaster Megyn Kelly declared that “he seems like an idiot.” Steve Bannon, a longtime adviser to the president, said on his War Room show that he is “not so sure it’s helpful to keep putting Markwayne Mullin on shows like Sean Hannity or even have him go on CNBC.” Mullin followed those wobbly appearances with testimony before the House Homeland Security Committee yesterday—and used nearly his entire opening statement to angrily justify flying on a government jet to see a college-football game in Louisiana less than 24 hours after the FAA ground stop had been lifted, as thousands of travelers remained stranded. “I wanted to be a good uncle and take my little niece, who has never been to an LSU game, and she’s a huge LSU fan, to a game,” he said. By then, the White House had already seemingly relieved Mullin from his role as the designated explainer of the mysterious outages, replacing him with Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, who brings a more lawyerly bearing. “Good move by the White House,” former Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt wrote on X as Clayton took the lead on Fox News. In a statement, DHS told me that “Mullin surrounds himself with a variety of experts” from across the department’s 22 agencies and components. “Secretary Mullin employs a management style that empowers his agency heads, his staff, and every individual,” the statement said, citing his track record on deportations, border security, and drug seizures. “The results speak for themselves.” D HS secretaries have to be conversant on a range of topics, such as airline travel, cybersecurity , and operations of the U.S. Secret Service. What has usually tripped up Mullin in his new role, especially among right-wing critics, has been his imprecise statements about immigration enforcement. Handling immigration might be the most politically charged part of his job, and partisans on all sides are looking for signifiers in every statement and utterance. During his confirmation hearing, Mullin told lawmakers that he wanted to turn down the visibility and temperature of Trump’s mass-deportation campaign, relaying the direction he had received from the White House following the killing of two U.S. citizens during an ICE crackdown in Minneapolis. Immigration arrests and deportations have reached record highs in recent months, but some of the president’s most ardent supporters—among them, loyalists to Noem —have retained their skepticism of Mullin. During his years in Congress, Mullin was one of the biggest supporters of Trump’s border wall, but he also spoke favorably of hardworking immigrants who stay out of trouble. Some of the gaffes and misstatements that Mullin has made over the past several weeks have fanned claims from hard-liners that he’s not as committed to mass deportations as Noem’s team. After Democrats’ historic midterm wins, Mullin said that Congress could work on immigration reform “where we can look at DACA and figure out a way that these individuals can become maybe legal permanent citizens or something like this.” There is no such thing as “legal permanent citizens” in U.S. immigration law, and Mullin appeared to conflate legal permanent residency with U.S. citizenship. But it was Mullin’s mention of President Obama’s Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program that triggered the greatest outrage on the right. Mullin said that some DACA recipients “may not even speak English or never even lived in their country,” apparently intending to say that such people spoke only English. Trump and others have insisted that the administration would not support “amnesty,” the proposals for legal pathways that hard-liners deplore, but that was the word Mullin used last week during an interview with Fox News when he meant to say “asylum,” the immigration process for border crossers who claim to be fleeing persecution in their home country. “If they want to talk about making people that enter this country here illegally legal, that’s a nonstarter,” Mullin told Laura Ingraham. “If they want to talk about how do we reform amnesty and how the port of entries work,” Mullin said before Ingraham cut in. Mullin has referred to gang members as “serious affiliated drug bangers” and used the term collateral criminals instead of collateral arrests —ICE’s term for people who were not the intended target of immigration raids but were swept up as well, regardless of whether they have criminal records. Mullin has also gotten in trouble for appearing to speak out of turn. After an ICE officer in Maine fatally shot a Colombian delivery driver on July 13 while his family was nearby, Mullin gave an order to suspend nonessential traffic stops. Immigration hard-liners protested to Trump, saying that the move made the administration look weak, and the next day, Trump reversed the order . T here’s been no indication that Trump is preparing to fire Mullin, despite calls on the right for his replacement. Getting another secretary nominated and confirmed in the Senate will become much more difficult after Democrats take control in January. Mullin has never committed the cardinal sin of Trumpism: disloyalty. And Trump himself misstates immigration law and facts almost every time he discusses the topic, layering his speeches with made-up numbers (“25 million people came in illegally”), unsubstantiated claims (immigrants sent from “insane asylums”), and flagrant lies (“they’re eating the dogs, the people that came in; they’re eating the cats”). Trump told 60 Minutes after the midterms that his immigration crackdown had been “too tough” and that he is open to working with Democrats. He then proceeded to name Stephen Miller, the driving force behind his mass-deportation campaign, as White House chief of staff. Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic nominee for speaker of the House, has said that he won’t work with Miller, calling him a “stone-cold racist.” Miller’s promotion may help Mullin keep his job a bit longer. The most hawkish voices in the MAGA movement want Trump to double down on mass deportations, and Mullin has demonstrated that he’s more than willing to continue on that course if the White House directs him to do so—even if he talks out of turn or flubs his interviews.

items.title: The Islands That Texas Wants From Mexico
items.description: D espite all of the disagreements and misunderstandings between the United States and Mexico, the two countries, until recently, seemed to at least agree on how to locate their border. It had, after all, been a settled matter of international law for more than 170 years, since the end of the Mexican-American War and the U.S. purchase of New Mexico. Then came an announcement late last month from Texas General Land Commissioner Dawn Buckingham. “I have a responsibility to protect every acre of state land,” she began. Buckingham went on to describe nine small, overgrown islands in the Rio Grande between the U.S. and Mexico, whose ownership, she wrote, had been “uncertain.” Her office, after being contacted by U.S. Customs and Border Protection, determined that the islands belonged to Texas. Buckingham said that the “strategically located lands”—roughly 66 acres in total—would soon be “accessed, monitored, and protected” by state and federal authorities. It seemed that the border was going to shift once again. Mexican officials, still trying to navigate the Trump administration’s periodic threats of an air strike, suddenly needed to take on a question that they thought had been resolved since before Abraham Lincoln took office: the contours of their own nation. Befuddled diplomats consulted with Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, who addressed the issue at a press conference by suggesting that her nation’s northern neighbor was playing politics. “They are in the midst of elections and are claiming that these islands are now part of Texas,” she said. “But they are not.” [ Read: The schism within the Trump administration on Mexico ] The Rio Grande islands—several dozen of them in total—have for years been an annoyance to members of the U.S. Border Patrol, who believe that human smugglers and drug traffickers use them as waypoints. Armed prison escapees from Mexico once hid on one of the islands; Mexican soldiers raided a “narco camp” on another; Border Patrol agents once rescued an 11-year-old Salvadoran girl from one. The dots of land are covered in long stalks of carrizo cane that gave criminal spotters a hidden vantage point for surveilling the border. Some used them to stash packages of cocaine. Rudy Karisch, a former chief of the Border Patrol’s Rio Grande Valley sector, remembers seeing the islands for the first time and puzzling over what to do about the unexpected nuisance. “The first thing I thought was, Why can’t we dredge them out and get rid of them? ,” he told me. It hasn’t been that simple. The islands were formed over years as the Rio Grande, like all rivers, moved sediment and carved a new course. In 1848’s Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, the two nations agreed that the border would remain in “the middle of that river, following the deepest channel.” But as the river moved, so did the border, periodically adding hundreds of acres to one country’s territory as it eroded the other’s. Sometimes, tracts of land disappeared under floodwaters. Those changes to the border could take years to resolve, but they were almost always handled amicably. Buckingham’s statement was different. It appeared to amount to a unilateral land grab. T he border’s original surveyors didn’t anticipate a shifting border. They didn’t care much for the border region at all. “Much of this country,” wrote Dr. Thomas Webb, one of the original border surveyors, “is a sterile waste, utterly worthless for any purpose than to constitute a barrier or natural line of demarcation between two neighboring nations.” But as the border became more important and surveyors became more precise, both countries began paying more attention to where the actual line was. In the 1880s, the U.S. and Mexico clashed over the ownership of 20-acre Beaver Island, just southeast of Roma, Texas. In 1889, the International Boundary Commission was formed to resolve future disputes; it was later renamed the International Boundary and Water Commission as it monitored the flows of binational rivers. In the 20th century, land shifted back and forth between the two nations, usually without major concerns from officials in Washington or Mexico City. The most recent time Americans unilaterally claimed territory across the border was in the 19th century. Now more than $1 million in freight crosses the border every minute. Mexican and American policy makers and intellectuals have long suggested that that entwined commercial relationship would lead to a more peaceful politics. In the Donald Trump era, that hasn’t always felt true. By the time Buckingham, a physician from Austin, took over the Texas General Land Office in 2023, the border was one of the most monitored, patrolled, and highly secured stretches of rural land in the world. It was also at the center of state and national political campaigns. She decided that it would be a top priority of her tenure. In October 2025, Buckingham received a request from U.S. Customs and Border Protection, which asked her to review 28 islands along the Rio Grande “whose ownership had not been definitively established,” she told me. “The request brought an important issue to our attention,” she said. “When ownership is unclear, it can create uncertainty about which country’s law-enforcement agencies have authority to access and operate on that property.” (CBP declined to comment.) Buckingham has sometimes worn a red Make America Texas cap, and in 2024, she purchased 1,400 acres of border land on the state’s behalf that she suggested could be used for a facility to process deportees as part of the president’s mass-deportation campaign. On other occasions, however, she has pushed back against the Trump administration, arguing, for example, that a border wall is not necessary in the Big Bend region of West Texas. In late October, she shared satellite imagery of the nine islands that appeared to show that they were north of the midway point in the Rio Grande. Buckingham cited the images as evidence that the islands belong to the United States. Buckingham told me that she is “not attempting to redraw the international boundary or replace the role of the IBWC. We are establishing the State of Texas’s ownership interest in property based on the records available to our agency.” But it’s unclear how claiming the island to be Texas property wouldn’t also change the international boundary, if the land isn’t already considered American. Mexican officials have become accustomed to threats of unilateral action from U.S. officials. Trump told Mexico’s president during the first week of his first term that he might send U.S. troops across the border to hunt down Mexican cartels. Later, he ruminated about shooting migrants in the legs and adding snakes and alligators to existing border infrastructure. [ Read: What I saw in Sinaloa ] But even Trump hasn’t talked about reapportioning land along the border. The federal government had long resolved borderland and border-water disputes through the IBWC, the binational commission of diplomats and engineers that is based in El Paso and Ciudad Juárez. Even as friction mounted between the two countries periodically over the past century, technocrats have quietly worked to settle disputes and maintain bilateral relations, no matter the political moment. Buckingham’s announcement took Mexican members of the IBWC by surprise, one Mexican official told me. (U.S. representatives on the IBWC declined to comment.) In her statement, Buckingham said that law-enforcement agents would be able to “patrol, inspect and clear (the islands) of any illegal activity.” It’s unclear whether agents have already been dispatched. If they were sent to land that wasn’t formally part of the United States, it might boost border enforcement, but it could also violate a long-standing treaty between the two countries. "The way we have resolved these issues over land has worked the same way for 137 years,” one Mexican official told me. In an instant, that appeared to be changing. T o get to the border islands from , say, Houston, you would need to head south on U.S. 77 past the Sarita checkpoint, where Border Patrol agents man a stretch of highway, 85 miles north of the Rio Grande. You would have to pass through—or over—the border wall, which in many places sits hundreds of meters north of the river. You would need to walk the arid no-man’s-land between the wall and the river. You would then need to take a short swim. You would, effectively, need to cross multiple borders to get to the border that Buckingham has claimed. As Mexico and the IBWC weighed how to respond to Buckingham’s claim over the islands, Texas politics were turned upside down . In a statewide rout of Republicans, Buckingham lost her election this month to a Democrat, Benjamin Flores. Now it will be Flores, a pig farmer raised in Mexico City, who will decide whether to pursue ownership of the islands. When I called Flores this week, he told me that he was puzzled by Buckingham’s claim. “To say that these islands belong to Texas now, without respect for a bilateral agreement, is pretty cavalier,” he said. “There’s a process to resolve these things, and I’ll respect the process.” Buckingham’s successor told me that he has questions about how Texas’s border acquisition came about and how much was spent on it. Flores said that he plans to look into the project with an eye for “waste, fraud, and abuse.” But even as Texas politics has changed, the occupant of the White House hasn’t. Trump and his administration have not addressed the fate of the islands directly. But the president has taken to Truth Social lately to warn of the “Huge CARAVANS” that “are forming and beginning their illegal march through Mexico.” Days after the election, Trump promoted to White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, his longtime aide who has previously pushed to conduct strikes on Mexican cartels. Miller in recent months has been making frequent calls to the U.S. ambassador in Mexico City to complain about border-crossing numbers. But he also celebrates how the border has been “sealed,” recently reposting on X a video of a quiet stretch of the Rio Grande. It was filmed not far from the islands.

items.title: The 2026 Atlantic Gift Guide
items.description: Welcome to The Atlantic ’s 2026 gift guide! Our editorial team has selected 55 gifts for this holiday season; find something to delight everyone in your life. The Quintessential Host The Best Cheese in America Courtesy of Jasper Hill Farm Not to brag, but I used to have an in with the best cheese in America. My best friend worked at Jasper Hill for many years. In that time, I became intimately acquainted with its funky, gooey, nutty, ashy products. Some of them, such as the cheddar and the blue, are the highest possible expression of cheeses you know and love. Others—the squashy Willoughby and molten Harbison—taste like nothing you’ve ever had before. If someone in your life throws dinner parties that seem unimprovable, give them a few months of Jasper Hill. — Lily Meyer , Staff Writer $105/month on Jasper Hill Farm Marionette Replicas Courtesy of Marionettes.cz Every time I have friends over and half-heartedly throw on some YouTube music videos, I think: If only I had $23,210 to buy the requisite set of replica marionettes, I would be entertaining these guys right now with a shot-perfect re-creation of “The Lonely Goatherd” from the 1965 film The Sound of Music. Granted, that’s a lot of money, and getting the goatherd’s yodeling to look just right will take significant practice, but it will be so worth it when your guests say, “What?” and also, “Why?” — Drew Goins , Senior Editor $23,210 on Marionettes.cz The Perfect Juicer Courtesy of Dreamfarm My household is such a big consumer of sour-sweet concoctions that we joke that citrus is the fifth element. Like fire, air, earth, and water, lemons resist taming: squirts in the eye, acid under the nails, seeds in the salad. But the Fluicer, a juice press that smashes with horizontal force, avoids mess and wastes no drop. Pour up your tangy treat of choice and celebrate man’s latest victory over nature. — Spencer Kornhaber , Staff Writer $19.99 on Dreamfarm Top-Tier Coffee Courtesy of Trade I am more pretentious and particular about my coffee than anything else. Imagine having coffee beans from all the best hipster roasters around the country brought to your doorstep each week. That’s what Trade offers. You fill out a questionnaire on how you take your coffee, what flavor profiles you prefer, and how adventurous you want to be. The company matches you with different shops that send you freshly roasted beans on the weekly. I’ve subscribed for years, and have expanded my palate every which way. — Matt Viser , Staff Writer $66 for a three-month subscription on Trade The Muscle Car of Espresso Machines Courtesy of Whole Latte Love Espresso lovers have plenty of cheap, one-touch, self-timing options for the home kitchen. But jeweled Nespresso pods and Breville automation have their limits when caffeine addiction succumbs to the obsessive quest for the perfect pour. The Profitec Go, a German-engineered, Italian-made machine, operates more like a classic stick-shift muscle car than a shiny new Tesla. Every part is adjustable—the pressure, the temperature, the timing—which makes each shot an aspirational leap for the unreachable ideal. The hardware heats up slower than the competition. But in a world of creeping mediocrity and oppressive efficiency, we all must choose where to make our stand. — Michael Scherer , Staff Writer $1,199 on Whole Latte Love Handcrafted Knives Courtesy of Everett Noel Knives Few tools are more essential to cooking than a good, sharp knife. Everett Noel, a cutler wunderkind, began making knives at 13, and taught himself how by watching YouTube videos. Fifteen years later, he has honed his craft into something sublime, and produces some seriously beautiful knives, including this paring knife . Based in the Sierra Nevada foothills, Everett makes each handle from locally sourced hardwood, much of it salvaged from fallen trees, and forges the blades from steel. The result is a functional work of art. — Sophia Grace Carter , Associate Editor $100–$725 on Everett Noel Knives The Silverware You Can Keep Gifting Courtesy of Sabre Paris This set will help you stop agonizing over what to get your kitchen-savvy friend for every gift-giving occasion. Sabre is known for its unique, stylish cutlery that comes in a bunch of colors and patterns. Pick one, and then give your friend something from the collection again and again. Bottle openers! Butter knives! Tart servers! More spoons! Soon, your friend will have a drawer full of matching tortoiseshell tableware, thanks to you. — Katie Anthony , Associate Editor $122.50 on Sabre Paris The Joy of Cooking Courtesy of Simon & Schuster Much like the Velveteen Rabbit knew he was loved because of his threadbareness, to know a cookbook is adored is to see it soiled with stains. My copy of The Joy of Cooking is splotched all over. When I was 19, my mother gave me this 1,000-page doorstopper, and since then, it’s taught me how to boil an egg, roll out fresh pasta, make Swedish meatballs, and perfect a bone broth. When people ask me, “Can I have your key-lime pie recipe?” I sheepishly admit that it’s not mine at all, but rather filched from the cookbook whose only misery is to be covered in food. — Andrea Valdez , Managing Editor $45 on Bookshop A Fun Cake Server Courtesy of Coming Soon A cake or pie server is one of those hyper-specific things—no one needs one, but without it, whenever dessert time rolls around, you are left either using a boring spatula or, worse, wrangling a piece of cake awkwardly using two forks, which usually ends with losing half the slice on the table. Nothing screams “fun host” more than a hand-shaped server! — Tina Zhou , Designer $50 on Coming Soon The Lifelong Student Your Own Ticker Courtesy of Tidbyt You know the ticker that scrolls through sports scores or stock prices at the bottom of your TV screen? Now you can have your own! The Tidbyt features a snazzy little display that zips through the weather forecast and news headlines. You can personalize it via an app; we use it to monitor real-time traffic, subway updates, and, most importantly, sports scores and standings. Need to know who is leading the American League East? Just wait a moment! But there is a downside: When the Patriots lost the Super Bowl this year, the Tidbyt’s score display felt like a relentless reminder (my sons and I turned the NFL app off until the new season). — Jonathan Lemire , Staff Writer $199 on Tidbyt A Whole Library Getty People often suggest books as gifts—why not get serious about it and buy an entire library? The Boston-based company Ars Libri acquires the libraries of the world’s greatest scholars, collectors, and curators when they retire, downsize, or die, and sells them to universities and libraries. But they will sell to you too! For about $730,000, you could buy a library comprising 500 key books on scientific knowledge from Enlightenment France, including a beautiful copy of Diderot’s Encyclopédie . Or, for just $285,000, you could have a library of 3,240 titles compiled by Sheldon Peck, a collector of Dutch Golden Age drawings. What else are you going to do with that spare room? — Sebastian Smee , Staff Writer $730,000 on Ars Libri A Custom Insect Specimen Courtesy of Lawrence Forcella For my husband’s 30th birthday, I asked Lawrence Forcella, otherwise known as the God of Insects, to frame two walking-leaf-bug specimens. He found me a male Pulchriphyllium bioculatum and a female Cryptophyllium celebicum , and set them in a custom frame for $240 (plus shipping) from somewhere in New York State. I don’t have my husband’s fondness for or fascination with insects, but even I love to look at them. They’re stunning. They’re unbelievable! Aliens on Earth. You’ll have to write to Mr. Forcella well in advance, because he’s an artist. — Kaitlyn Tiffany , Staff Writer Varies on God of Insects A Guide to American Goods Courtesy of Crafted With Pride I thought this was a weird gift when someone gave it to me, but it has actually changed my life, by which I mean: how I shop, dress, and think about my country. This is the most comprehensive guide to wearable goods made in America, including sunglasses, T-shirts, blankets, and custom cowboy boots. If you’re not much of a shopper, you’ll be putting together a story about how people keep a tradition alive that used to define this country. If you are one, you’ll discover truly original designs, and understand better why you might want to pay a little extra for them. — Hanna Rosin , Senior Editor $39.95 on Crafted With Pride Not Your Average Candle Courtesy of JD + Kate Industries The history enthusiast in your life has enough books and maps. What they really want, even if they don’t know it yet, is a tiny wax tableau that they can light on fire to “watch the Roman forum melt into a puddle.” Or to find out “what it smells like when you dump 46 tons of tea into Boston Harbor during a New England winter.” Literary types might prefer to contemplate the “smoking ruins” of Mr. Rochester’s Thornfield estate. As the company puts it: “Sometimes when you lock your wife in the attic and propose to the governess, your house gets burned down. Actions have consequences!” — Karen Ostergren , Deputy Copy Chief $25 on JD + Kate Industries A Journal to Remember What—And Where—You Read Courtesy of Papier After my grandmother passed away, we went through all of her books and found that she had written notes inside hundreds of covers. Yes, she jotted down her thoughts on the book at hand, but she would also note the location of her grandchildren at the time of reading, her favorite lines, who recommended the title, and even where she was sitting when she finished the book. I’ve taken up the practice, but a reading journal also keeps these notes in one place. A book is as much about the moment in which you read it as anything else. — Grace Buono , Assistant Editor $38 on Papier The Ultimate Board Game Courtesy of GMT Games This two-player, world-encompassing, multi-hour card-and-board game—in which one person plays for global domination as the U.S.S.R., and the other as the United States—had me, a generally very nice person, screaming at my partner about approaching DEFCON 1. Don’t buy Twilight Struggle for your casual board-gamer friend. It’s a gift for board-game sociopaths who feel invigorated by infinite numbers of play decisions about historical events from 1945 to 1989. For the highest tier of board-game evangelists in your life, you can preorder the 20th-anniversary edition . — Shan Wang , Programming Director $94 on Amazon A Better Way Down Courtesy of Aspen Paragliding I hike up Ajax Mountain in Aspen, Colorado, a few times a week. It’s a three-mile hike with 3,200 feet of elevation. For my birthday, my wife gave me a tandem-paragliding flight (from Aspen Paragliding). So one morning, I hiked to the top, met my pilot, strapped myself to him, and ran off the side of the mountain. It was exhilarating, surprisingly peaceful, and an entirely new way to see a mountain I thought I knew. It also beats taking the gondola down. The only downside: I couldn’t bring my dog. — Russell Shaw , Contributing Writer $400 on Aspen Paragliding A Written Time Capsule Courtesy of Tamara Shopsin Nearly everyone wants more time, but no one has figured out how to tie a bow on it. Thankfully, a sense of time affluence usually has less to do with quantity than with quality—how our days are lived and remembered. For this, there is a gift! Tamara Shopsin’s elegant, clothbound five-year diary may look dainty, but it can hold the details of every day across five years. I’m on my third, and I’ve pushed this book into more hands than I can count. Not everyone takes to it, but those who do appreciate the way that a simple chronicle of an ordinary Tuesday delineates and enriches what might otherwise get lost with time. — Emily Bobrow , Senior Editor $29.95 on Amazon The Person Who Has Everything Ridiculously Fragrant Laundry Detergent Courtesy of Tyler Candle Store Tyler Glamorous Wash laundry detergent is something that no one in their right mind would buy for themselves. I don’t own this detergent; it’s far too expensive to purchase, and I am in my right mind. However, the last time I visited wealthy friends, I found myself huffing their bath towels like they were doused in nitrous oxide. This is the most perfumed product civilization has ever created. What does it smell like? Rich people’s towels. You can get a sample set of three scents for $24–$30 (plus shipping). You’ll be shocked at how little detergent this buys! — Caity Weaver , Staff Writer $30 on Tyler Candle Store Limited-Edition Oreos Courtesy of Oreo Food seems like an undeniable gift in theory, but rarely in practice: Your cousin’s girlfriend inevitably has some allergy you were unaware of, making your homemade treat a biohazard. But a weirdly flavored prepackaged snack is fun—even for those who don’t actually want to eat it. I consider myself an Oreo-cookie connoisseur, and I taste-test every limited-edition cookie as soon as it’s released. This year brought a BTS-branded, brown-sugar-pancake flavor to shelves (pretty good), as well as a chicken-and-waffles cookie (vile). My friends insisted that a Marvel Comics–themed creation from earlier this year tasted like garlic—I didn’t agree, but the mere fact that I brought them such a peculiar Oreo to try was well received. It’s sometimes more fun to ponder whether a cookie will taste good than it is to actually try it. — Allegra Frank , Senior Editor $10–$42.99 on Oreo Peepy Courtesy of Item Label Peepy is a little stuffed creature whose body usually consists of two orbs. I say “usually” because there are, in fact, many different Peepy variants, some of which get pretty abstract. The standard Peepy is white with black spots, like a cow, but there’s also Snakepy , a Peepy in the process of being swallowed by a snake, and Island Peepy , which appears to be sprouting a palm tree. My little cousin got a kick out of the now-sold-out Ice Cream Peepy . I have a hunch that there’s a Peepy for everyone. — Will Gottsegen , Staff Writer $30 on Item Label The Best Peanut Butter in the World Courtesy of Teddie The very best peanut butter, perhaps even the best food in general, comes in a thick glass jar with a bear reclined across the label: Teddie Peanut Butter. Teddie’s—those in the know make it possessive, as if the product was the bear’s own—contains just two ingredients, peanuts and salt, ground into a thick goop in Everett, Massachusetts. Last year, the family behind Teddie’s compiled a series of peanut-butter-forward recipes—cookies, fudge, “Asian sesame chicken meatballs”—and although I’m sure they’re excellent, let’s not kid ourselves. The best way to enjoy Teddie’s is on your feet, spoon in one hand, jar in the other, refrigerator light dancing across the glass. — Andrew Aoyama , Deputy Managing Editor $4.79 on Target A Professional Home Organizer Getty The dream for everything I buy is that it will fix my life. New pants, new mascara, that 3 p.m. latte. And they do fix it—for a moment. But one purchase keeps giving: a home organizer. She emptied my cabinets, my kid’s 2 million toy baskets, and my husband’s 3 million hobby boxes. Then she put everything back, neatly labeled and easily discoverable. She even revealed more storage space, which, in New York City, is akin to discovering untapped oil. Organizers are pricey, but look: This person fixed my life. Find a service in your loved one’s city, and they’ll be thanking you for days to come. — Serena Dai , Senior Editor A Cuckoo Clock Courtesy of Muji When I first encountered this adorable Muji device and its tiny resident bird at my friend’s house, I coveted it immediately. My husband wasn’t convinced. Wouldn’t it be annoying? My answer, now that I own one, is a confident no: This clock is perfect . It is tall and skinny, like a cuckoo townhouse, and looks stylish on a bookshelf or gallery wall. Every 30 and 60 minutes, the bird lets out a string of chirps, but thanks to the built-in light sensor, she doesn’t sing at night. Just in case, there is a mute button. — Elaine Godfrey , Staff Writer $79.90 on Muji A Home for Their Butter Courtesy of Blake ’n’ Grey A wisely chosen present will remind the recipient of your affection and good taste every time they use it, so it’s advisable to give them something that they can reach for daily. Consider the butter crock: a two-piece ceramic creation, at once a sculpture and a feat of engineering, that uses a water seal to keep butter soft and fresh and spreadable outside the fridge. Variations of this fabulous artifact are available on Etsy for as little as $30. Give a butter crock, and the recipient will think of you at the sight of butter melting on bread. — Gisela Salim-Peyer , Associate Editor $33 on Etsy A Post-Shower Luxury Courtesy of Serene Life Every so often, I receive a present so indulgent that I never would have bought it myself. This towel warmer, which my cousin got me as a (literal) housewarming gift, is exactly that. Do I need to be wrapped in toasted fabric every time I emerge from the shower? Probably not. Are there other more practical things with which I should be filling my still-not-fully-furnished apartment? Definitely. I owned a towel warmer before I owned a coat rack. But this thing makes every dark, cold morning a little better. — Kelsey Ables , Staff Writer $99.99 on Amazon Perfume for the It Girl Courtesy of Parfums de Marly We all have that one friend who’s the group chat’s It Girl. My friend introduced me to Delina Exclusif Parfum Parfums de Marly, and I’ve been obsessed ever since. Look, I debated even mentioning the perfume in this gift guide. So this is my present to you: Delina Exclusif Parfum smells like the richest and most refined form of femininity. And in the words of my friend, who, by the way, never, ever steers me wrong: When it’s the good stuff, you only have to spray it once . — Jenisha Watts , Staff Writer $450 on Parfums de Marly Dessert in a Bottle Courtesy of Transcendence Coffee Gulab Jamun is one of the best Indian desserts—warm, spongy, and rich with hints of rose and cardamom. Imagine that in your coffee (or pancakes, or ice cream). I love that the spices in this syrup are not overpowering, and that you can control how sweet you want your latte. Delicious! — Akshita Chandra , Art Director $19 on Transcendence Coffee The Person Who Needs to Touch Grass Low-Pressure Painting Courtesy of Tobios Kits Once you’ve committed to touching grass , this gift can help you, and others, with what to do next. Look at the grass, your dog, or just out the window. Consider the shadows, textures, and colors. Then, if you’re like me (meaning untrained in watercolor technique), use this set to paint in a low-pressure way. The special water brush allows you to get going without any additional containers, and check out the clever wristband water blotter. Remember, if you get creatively stuck, you can always pull up a YouTube painting tutorial and keep one foot in the digital world. — Jocelyn Frank , Senior Producer $34 on Amazon A New Way to Read Courtesy of Xteink Maybe you’ve heard that Americans are doing too much doomscrolling and not enough reading . To get off your screen, consider buying … another screen! This e-reader, which is the size of a credit card, has changed my relationship with reading. Unlike e-readers with distracting features, this one is bare-bones. The best thing about this ridiculous gadget is that it magnetically snaps to the back of an iPhone, making it easy to get some reading in whenever you have a little bit of free time. Since I bought an Xteink, my screen time has decreased by 25 minutes a day—and I haven’t had to put my phone down. — Saahil Desai , Senior Editor $69 on Amazon Sapphire Hunting in Montana Courtesy of Gem Mountain Sapphire Mine The first sapphires were discovered in the Big Sky state in the 1860s by miners looking for gold. Montana sapphires are extremely distinctive: They are typically gray-blue before heat treatment, but they can also be pink, orange, or even, adorably, bicolored. Today, several mines allow summer tourists to buy a big bag of sapphire-bearing gravel and pan for stones themselves, before sending off any gem-grade discoveries for heating and cutting. Even better, most of the sites are so deep in the countryside that there’s no cellphone reception. — Helen Lewis , Staff Writer $55 per bucket on Gem Mountain Rad Gloves Courtesy of Freezy Freakies I was a kid of the ’80s, and in the winter, that meant snow days equaled endless snowball fights. This was pre-streaming, pre-Netflix, and pre-internet. Outside was way more fun than inside. And when Freezy Freaky gloves and their newfangled technology came about, I was desperate for a pair, in particular the Robot gloves . Their full retro glory reveals itself only once they are out in the cold (below 40 degrees). They are still rad, and would be a totally awesome gift for someone in your life who needs to get outside and touch snow, whether they are 6 or 60. — Claudine Ebeid , Executive Producer $29–39 on Freezy Freakies A Simple Watch Courtesy of CW&T Sometimes, you just need to tell the time. Watch snobs and tech junkies alike will appreciate the Solid State Watch, a reimagination of the ubiquitous Casio F-91W, a reliable workhorse of a wristwatch that has remained unchanged since its 1989 release. Part experimental art, part utility item, the artist-engineers Che-Wei Wang and Taylor Levy permanently entombed this watch in resin, so it has no buttons, no fancy functions, and no way of changing its 10-year battery. The machine will just keep ticking and ticking through the next decade, grounding you in a way that only a good timepiece can. — Fiza Kuzhiyil , Assistant Editor $199 on CW&T A Tea Era Courtesy of Tezumi Tea Every person deserves a tea era, and I don’t just mean guzzling Starbies matcha lattes with five pumps of vanilla syrup. For tea newbies and veterans alike, I recommend the Shudashi Kokudei Tokoname tea set from Tezumi. The set comes with one well-made Tokoname-yaki kyusu, a traditional Japanese ceramic teapot, and four elegant porcelain teacups. Making a good pot of sencha or gyokuro or houjicha (all of which Tezumi also sells) is a great way to slow down and be in the real world for a moment, and, perhaps, to share that moment with people you love. — Vann R. Newkirk II , Senior Editor $148 on Tezumi Tea The Book of Distraction Courtesy of Goods for the Study Look, we all have bad days. But we also all have certain people in our circles who can’t let them go, and for those people, this slightly passive-aggressive gift offers a place to vent that isn’t your ear at happy hour. Encourage the frustrated complainer in your life to release their troubles into this Accumulated Grievances notebook. Journaling has many proven mental and emotional benefits, one being that it boosts self-awareness, so your loved one may come to realize how solipsistic they’re being. — Sophie Gilbert , Staff Writer $10 on Amazon A Fishing Rod for the Everyman Courtesy of Pflueger Largemouth bass are the people’s fish. They can be found in remote southern farm ponds, sprawling western reservoirs, and Central Park. The pursuit of largemouth can be a desperately complicated (and terribly expensive) affair if you want it to be—but the truth is that bass are quite easy to catch from shore with simple gear and minimal effort. Pflueger has long made high-quality but affordable rods and reels: This 6-foot-6-inch medium combo , some eight-pound monofilament line , a pack of size 1/0 “octopus” hooks , and a few bags of five-inch “Senko” plastic worms (rig them “whacky” style) is all anyone needs to get started. — Tyler Austin Harper , Staff Writer $95.99 on Pflueger Whimsical Vases Courtesy of the MoMA Design Store Last holiday season, I bought these mini glass vases for my mom and husband (read: also for myself), and they were a huge hit. They’re colorful, adorable, and affordable, and they add a bit of whimsy to nearly every part of your home. Sometimes, we use them to dot our bookshelves, and other times, we line them up on our kitchen table, making a rushed weeknight dinner feel just a little more bright. My kids especially love walking through our neighborhood to gather individual tiny flowers to fill different vases. — Ashley Parker , Staff Writer $20 on MoMA Design Store The Cadillac of Binoculars Courtesy of B&H More and more young people are touching grass by way of birding . Your loved one could be next! For all-purpose birding and nature observation, 8x42 binoculars (with eight times magnification and a 42-millimeter lens) are a great bet and come at virtually every price point. My birding sources tell me that Vortex offers the best value (I once tried the Vortex Diamondbacks and loved them), but for the best possible vision, this Zeiss pair is the way to go. — Rachel Gutman-Wei , Senior Editor $2,999.99 on B&H The Practical One The Communal Outdoor Couch Courtesy of Kelty Lounging around a campfire, at the beach, or at an outdoor concert should be a communal activity, but the one-seater camping chair renders it a curiously solo affair. Enter the Lowdown Couch. Sturdy and comfortable, it seats three adults, or some combo of adults, kids, and pets. Although it’s not exactly light, it won’t tax you on a short walk, and you don’t need an engineering degree to fold it up. But the couch’s true value is in making you friends. Everyone will want to sit on it, first for the novelty, then for the obvious reason. Why, indeed, isn’t this standard hanging-out gear? — Evan McMurry , Senior Editor $149.96 on Amazon A Lazy Cat Lover’s Dream Courtesy of Whisker I love cats because they’re awesome—and because I’m lazy. Dogs are marvelous creatures, but you have to walk them no matter the time or weather. Cats are tidier, but we do have to scoop and change icky litter. No more! The Litter-Robot 4 and LitterHopper are great gifts for any cat owner. The Litter-Robot senses when your cat has, ah, visited; empties clumps into a container; and the LitterHopper (sold separately) adds fresh litter. An app tells you when to empty the waste drawer and replenish the hopper. They’re not cheap, but cats are worth it. — Tom Nichols , Staff Writer $699 on Amazon A Matchmaker Getty This one’s a high-risk, high-reward gift. The risk is that your family member or loved one might get super offended that you think they can’t find love on their own. The potential reward? A lifetime of happiness! There are a million options when it comes to matchmakers, but Liv Schreiber’s company Hot and Social just started a matchmaking service that seems promising. — Annie Joy Williams , Assistant Editor Varies on Hot and Social More Than a Candle Courtesy of Anthropologie Most people probably don’t understand why someone would need an expensive substitute for a matchbox—but if you’re afraid of fire (as I am) or have a fluffy-tailed cat with limited spatial awareness (as I do), a candle warmer is a revelation. It’s basically a heat lamp that allows you to release a candle’s scent without an open flame. And if your gift recipient hates candles or is fine with matches, it looks like a beautiful table lamp. — Rose Horowitch , Staff Writer $58 on Anthropologie Bento Boon Courtesy of Japanese Taste Maybe you’ve noticed that everybody—your co-worker, your high-school friend, your mom’s suburban mah-jongg club—is going to Japan lately. That is a long journey, and an expensive one. But for roughly $50, you can gift a piece of Japanese dinnerware to a friend without needing to travel farther than your front door. These two-tier bento boxes, made in Japan, are stainless steel (easy to sanitize and odor resistant) with a divider to prevent foods from mixing for the picky eater. They’re sleek, compact, and useful for just about anybody who needs to pack a meal on the go. Plus, any money saved from not buying lunch can go toward that plane ticket! — Stephanie Bai , Senior Associate Editor $49 on Japanese Taste A Sleek Bedside Assistant Courtesy of Loftie As a recovering doomscroller, I’ve tried to make my phone less essential to my morning and bedtime routines. About a year ago, I bought a very good alarm clock and bedside lamp that helped—all while making my nightstand much prettier in the process. Every morning, I wake up to calming sounds and light that gradually brightens like a sunrise, inspired by destinations such as Joshua Tree and Fiji. And at night, I program a little bedtime appetizer of soothing stories, meditations, and lullabies as the lamp shifts to warm, ambient colors that encourage sleep. They made both ends of my day feel a bit gentler and more elevated. — Janay Kingsberry , Staff Writer $199.99 on Loftie An Electric Gargoyle Courtesy of GOOTOP Who knew that the sound of love was actually a quick and clarion zap ? Listen, I know your loved one does not like mosquitos, gnats, or other tiny airborne menaces. Every zap is a reminder that a merciless electric gargoyle is attentive to its duty. This bug zapper is great for a patio or yard, though I’ve used mine as a satisfying nuclear option against fruit flies in the kitchen. And sure, it’s not the most aesthetic gift, but bug bites aren’t stylish either. — Bhumika Tharoor , Managing Editor $39.99 on Amazon A Ritual for Your Candle Courtesy of Candlefy Buying yourself a nice scented candle is already a once-a-year luxury—or so the voice in my head chides me as I purchase a new one every few weeks. But buying a special tool kit to take care of your fancy candles and turn lighting them into a small evening ritual? That’s just a bridge too far to get for yourself, which is, of course, what makes it the perfect gift. — Marie-Rose Sheinerman , Assistant Editor $19.99 on Candlefy Better Tools Courtesy of Fiskars Most of us have a household drawer filled with a dubious collection of tools accumulated over time, including wobbly scissors and maybe a clunky old box cutter. Why not make life a bit better with some quality cutting tools, such as the Fiskars shop shears or folding utility knife ? I replaced our old scissors with these shears years ago, and actually love when any cutting needs to be done. The blades are sharp and strongly connected for precise cuts. And the folding utility knife is comfortable and a joy to use. — Alan Taylor , Senior Editor $16.89 on Amazon Boots Really Made for Walking Courtesy of Dr. Martens Do you want to feel like a superhero with the power to confidently walk through a blizzard without slipping? If so, I’d highly recommend a pair of Dr. Martens boots. I bought my first pair back in 2019, and they remain one of the best gifts I’ve ever gotten myself. When the next snowstorm hits, you’ll wish you had a pair of durable and reliable shoes. — Michael Blackmon , Senior Associate Editor $210 on Dr. Martens The Creative Person A Four-Day Pass to the Best, Weirdest Musical Festival Courtesy of Big Ears Festival For a long weekend every spring, the best place in the world to hear live music is Knoxville, Tennessee. I’ve never quite figured out how to describe Big Ears, a festival that includes jazz, indie rock, contemporary classical, folk, and ambient music, but you could do worse than calling it NPR-core. Perhaps the best endorsement is that you stand a good chance of sitting or standing next to an off-duty headlining artist as they intently take in another show on the lineup. — David A. Graham , Staff Writer $450–$550 on Big Ears Festival An Eye-Popping Print Courtesy of Julia Foote Wall decor is a source of stress for me. One section of my room has been devoted to the same set of postcards pretty much since I went to college, but I wasn’t sure how to curate more things that felt like me. Enter the farmers’ market near my apartment—which is more of a market for stuff at this point—where I found some beautiful, eye-popping prints. They feel like a step up art-wise, without being overly snooty, and they really brighten up a room. For another unique option, my friend makes these gorgeous, quilt-inspired ones. — Elise Hannum , Associate Editor Varies on Julia Foote Bookplates Courtesy of Morgane Rospars These limited-edition bookplates are designed by Morgane Rospars (“a Breton woman living in exile in Le Havre”!) and can be customized with the recipient’s name. If you have room in the budget, you can commission an original design themed around your memories, hobbies, favorite artists; for a bit less, you can throw in an ink pad instead. — Sophia Nguyen , Staff Writer Starting at 75€ on Morgane Rospars Tree of Life Pitcher Courtesy of Gunia In February 2020, less than a year into his presidency, Volodymyr Zelensky gifted Pope Francis a ceramic pot from Gunia Project, one of Ukraine’s coolest young design houses. Two years later, when Russia invaded Ukraine, Gunia began to reflect the horrors of the war and Ukraine’s hope for victory in its ceramics, jewelry, clothing, and accessories. One incongruous and unforgettable design depicted an angelic figure holding a Molotov cocktail. The company’s co-founder Natasha Kamenska was a frequent presence in Zelensky’s fortified compound during the first two years of the Russian invasion, when she worked as a stylist for the first lady of Ukraine. — Simon Shuster , Staff Writer $200 on Gunia Project An Actually Unique Tote Courtesy of the LACMA Store I might count the curtains among my favorite objects inside the new wing at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. The textile designer Reiko Sudo used a process called sputtering to deposit a film of metal onto a thin layer of polyester, creating a gauzy, transparent fabric that defends artwork from UV light while giving off a purplish, metallic shimmer. These pleated, collapsible totes are made of the same material, and, I suppose, will protect your rare books and other delicate possessions that deserve better sun protection. — Francesca Billington , Copy Editor $150 on LACMA Store Pet Portrait Courtesy of JesseHotshoePhoto Commissioning a portrait of your loved one’s furry companion is a perfect way to honor the deep bond between a pet and their owner. It also acknowledges that, for many people, pets are an important (dare I say, equally important) part of the family unit, even if they are woefully underrepresented in the picture frames dotting our homes. I recommend using a shop like this one, which will paint the portrait by hand using watercolors, rather than printing off a digital—and potentially AI-generated—design. — Madison Hahamy , Assistant Editor $19.95–$339.95 on Etsy A Life-Crisis Solver Courtesy of Pioneer DJ For people nearing 30, a lifestyle change can sometimes quell the fear of aging. Some decide to settle down and become parents—rarer amid our “romance slump”—whereas others start running marathons, each mile inching them closer to a knee replacement. If someone you know suddenly appears with chick-like hair, talks about a club’s “great sound system,” and ultimately looks like a Brat-summer reenactor, they might be in need of a DJ controller, such as Pioneer’s DDJ-FLX4. Get your life back together at 140 beats per minute. — Álex Maroño Porto , Associate Editor $329 on Pioneer DJ

items.title: Zio/électrification rurale : La population donne son appréciation du projet Cizo
items.description: Tsévié, 18 nov. (ATOP) – Un groupe de journalistes de la presse publique et privée, curieux de constater les effets du projet d’électrification rurale Cizo, a effectué, le lundi 12 novembre, une tournée dans quatre villages de la commune Zio 1. De Koklonyipé à Kôdzo, en passant par Havé et Adangbé Lakotor, les témoignages recueillis révèlent les changements apportés par l’éclairage solaire dans le quotidien des populations. A Adangbé Lakotor, Ayaki Hezouwè, cultivateur, évoque avec satisfaction la sécurité qu’offre désormais la lumière à son ménage. Le soir, les habitations sont éclairées et les téléphones portables peuvent être rechargés sans difficulté. « Nous nous sentons plus en sécurité depuis que CIZO nous a apporté la lumière », témoigne-t-il. A Koklonyipé, Amedetonyo Komi Dodzi, agriculteur-éleveur, apprécie particulièrement les possibilités offertes à ses enfants. Grâce à l’éclairage à domicile, ceux-ci peuvent désormais étudier et réviser leurs leçons après la tombée de la nuit. A Kôdzo, c’est le commerce qui profite de cette énergie. Adonkor Akoele, commerçante, affirme que la lumière lui permet de poursuivre ses ventes au-delà de 18 heures, avec une augmentation de son chiffre d’affaires. De son côté, Togbui Noukounou Koffi, tradithérapeute, souligne les économies réalisées sur l’achat des piles traditionnelles. Lancé en 2017 par le gouvernement, le projet CIZO, qui signifie « allumer », vise à faciliter l’accès à l’électricité en milieu rural à travers des kits solaires à paiement échelonné. Selon les données présentées lors de la tournée, plus de 300 000 foyers en ont déjà bénéficié. ATOP/MG/MD

Journée des Forces armées : le Président Bassirou Diomaye Faye tend la main à la CEDEAO face aux menaces aux frontières
items.description: Pour la 25e Journée des Forces armées, célébrée au camp Dial Diop, le Président Bassirou Diomaye Diakhar Faye, Chef suprême des Armées, a rendu hommage aux soldats tombés, blessés ou éprouvés, et salué les chefs d’état-major de la CEDEAO présents avec qui il souhaite collaborer pour renforcer la sécurité aux frontières. C'est un rendez-vous que le calendrier républicain sénégalais place parmi ses plus solennels. Pour la 25e édition de la Journée des Forces armées, le Président Bassirou Diomaye Diakhar Faye s'est présenté ce matin devant les troupes alignées au quartier Dial Diop, entouré du Premier ministre, du président de l'Assemblée nationale, du ministre des Forces armées et de la haute hiérarchie militaire. Dans les tribunes, des chefs d'état-major venus de plusieurs pays de la CEDEAO, des anciens en tenue de cérémonie et des familles de militaires. Le Chef de l'État a commencé par rappeler les origines de cette journée : « Il est des dates qui continuent, au fil des générations, d'éclairer le destin d'une Nation. Le 10 novembre 1960 est de celles-là. » Quelques mois après l'indépendance, la remise du drapeau du 1er Régiment des Tirailleurs sénégalais au 1er Bataillon d'infanterie avait marqué, selon lui, « une étape fondatrice dans l'édification de notre Armée nationale ». Il a ajouté que « la jeune République sénégalaise affirmait ainsi sa volonté d'assumer pleinement ses responsabilités en matière de défense nationale ». Cette cérémonie, a-t-il souligné, est d'abord celle de la gratitude envers « celles et ceux qui, au nom de la Nation, ont fait le choix exigeant du service commandé, de la discipline et du sacrifice ». « Le monde a profondément changé » Le Président a ensuite dressé un tableau sans fard de l'environnement stratégique. « Le monde a profondément changé. L'émergence et l'affirmation de la puissance, la remise en cause de l'ordre multilatéral, la multiplication des espaces contestés, le délitement progressif des mécanismes multilatéraux de solidarité et les phénomènes transfrontaliers constituent les traits marqueurs d'une géopolitique mondiale plus que tumultueuse. » La région n'est pas à l'abri : « La persistance du terrorisme et de l'extrémisme violent, l'essor des trafics illicites, la criminalité transnationale organisée et la multiplication des foyers d'instabilité exercent une pression croissante sur nos États et sur les conditions de vie de nombreuses populations. » À ces menaces s'ajoutent, a-t-il énuméré, « les effets des dérèglements climatiques, les tensions autour des ressources, certaines vulnérabilités économiques et sociales, ainsi que les risques émergents dans les domaines cybernétique et informationnel ». Il a pointé une faille précise : « Les groupes armés et les réseaux criminels exploitent la mobilité transfrontalière, les fragilités de certains territoires et les insuffisances de coordination entre les dispositifs nationaux. » D'où son appel à « la mobilisation des énergies et des capacités régionales par le renforcement de notre anticipation, la connaissance approfondie des menaces et l'opérationnalisation de nos mécanismes de réponse ». L'histoire comme argument pour l'unité Pour justifier ce « sursaut régional », le chef de l'État a convoqué l'histoire. « Bien avant la constitution de nos États modernes, notre région était un espace de circulation, d'échanges et de solidarités humaines. Les frontières ont consacré nos souverainetés ; elles n'ont effacé ni les liens familiaux, ni les relations économiques, ni les héritages culturels partagés. » De cette proximité naît, selon lui, « une responsabilité particulière dans la recherche de la paix et dans la prévention des crises ». Il a rappelé que le Sénégal « n'a cessé de s'engager en faveur de la sécurité collective, dans le prolongement d'une longue tradition de solidarité africaine », et que ses soldats ont pris part, « aux côtés de leurs frères d'armes des pays de la sous-région, à différents engagements opérationnels ». Ces expériences partagées constituent à ses yeux « un acquis précieux sur lequel la coopération militaire régionale pourrait s'adosser pour franchir de nouvelles étapes ». Sur les secousses politiques qui traversent la sous-région, le Président a choisi la prudence : « Les recompositions politiques et institutionnelles que connaît notre sous-région exigent de la lucidité et du discernement. Elles nous invitent à préserver les voies du dialogue, à entretenir les relations de confiance et à rechercher patiemment les convergences nécessaires à une sécurité collective régionale dynamique. » Un message direct aux chefs d'état-major de la CEDEAO S'adressant ensuite aux chefs d'état-major des pays voisins, il a salué une présence « remarquée » qui « témoigne aussi de la fraternité qui unit nos pays et de la richesse des expériences accumulées et partagées depuis plusieurs décennies d'engagements communs ». Il a décrit les contours d'une coopération concrète : « Elles doivent conjuguer préparation opérationnelle et coopération renforcée. Cela suppose une meilleure maîtrise de nos capacités, des échanges de renseignements par des canaux appropriés et l'organisation d'exercices conjoints pour renforcer la confiance mutuelle. » Il a aussi défendu l'idée d'une autonomie stratégique régionale et continentale. Cette ambition, a-t-il précisé, « demande des personnels qualifiés, des capacités d'anticipation, des équipements adaptés et des mécanismes de financement et de soutien à la hauteur des missions confiées aux forces ». Elle exige aussi « des partenariats internationaux équilibrés, respectueux de nos priorités et attentifs au développement de compétences durables ». L'hommage aux morts, aux blessés et aux anciens Le ton s'est fait plus grave lorsque le Président a évoqué les disparus. « En ce jour particulier de commémoration, nos pensées vont d'abord à nos soldats tombés dans l'accomplissement de leur noble devoir. Je m'incline avec une profonde émotion devant leur mémoire. » Il a dit partager « la peine de leurs parents et frères d'armes », en leur témoignant « la reconnaissance de la Nation toute entière pour les sacrifices consentis au nom des idéaux de paix, de concorde et de solidarité ». Les militaires blessés, malades ou éprouvés ont eu leur part d'attention : « Le courage et l'esprit de sacrifice qui les a toujours animés sont à saluer. Je leur réaffirme toute notre compassion et leur adresse mes vœux de prompt rétablissement. » Aux « grands Anciens » présents, il a réservé un mot personnel : « J'éprouve une grande fierté de vous voir parmi nous car votre présence est de celles qui rassure. Merci d'être restés fidèles aux serments d'engagement, de discipline et de dignité qui ne vous ont jamais quittés, même après l'uniforme. Vous constituez un modèle à bien des égards. »

items.title: Orpailleurs : Retrouver un revenu après la Guinée
items.description: © JDM L’accueil au Mali des orpailleurs venus de Guinée mobilise les autorités et les humanitaires. Une fois les retours organisés, retrouver un revenu reste le défi de travailleurs et de familles, dont les parcours interrogent l’accès à l’emploi, l’encadrement de l’orpaillage et la coopération régionale. « Si nous rentrons sans accompagnement ni dispositif d’encadrement, la situation risque d’être très compliquée. » Rencontré par Journal du Mali le samedi 14 novembre sur le site de Ouézzindougou, près de Bamako, Sawadogo Emmanuel pense déjà à l’après. L’affluence y était en baisse. Ce Burkinabè, diplômé en Lettres modernes depuis 2023 de l’Université Joseph Ki-Zerbo, pratiquait l’orpaillage près de Siguiri. Il souhaitait gagner sa vie et soutenir les siens. Un groupe de 1 557 ressortissants ouest-africains, jugés et condamnés à Conakry puis libérés, a été conduit le 14 novembre à Kourémalé. Le transfert a été coordonné avec les représentations diplomatiques concernées. Pour les pays d’origine, l’organisation du retour pose aussi la question des moyens d’existence que ces travailleurs pourront retrouver. Conakry présente les opérations comme une lutte contre l’orpaillage illégal. Dans un communiqué du 12 novembre, le gouvernement guinéen a donné un bilan provisoire de 10 morts et de 13 blessés lors d’affrontements survenus la veille à Balato, pendant une opération de contrôle. Les autorités judiciaires ont été saisies. Sawadogo Emmanuel situe, lui, son départ à la fin d’octobre. Il dénonce des violences et des destructions de matériels, des accusations qui restent à corroborer. Au Mali, l’assistance répond aux besoins immédiats. Selon leur note opérationnelle du 12 novembre, la Croix-Rouge malienne et le CICR ont organisé une réponse associant alimentation, eau, soins et rétablissement des liens familiaux. Du 5 au 12 novembre, les volontaires ont distribué plus de 16 000 repas chauds à Bamako et dans ses environs. Le 14 novembre, Emmanuel insistait sur le manque de toilettes. Henri Kaboré affirmait manger à sa faim, mais évoquait les bousculades liées à l’affluence. Le 18 novembre, le site principal était démantelé. Le CECOGEC recensait 467 personnes à la Maison des jeunes d’Ouinzindougou et 20 Burkinabè à Kourémalé. Revenus À 21 ans, Henri Kaboré porte déjà une responsabilité familiale. Aîné d’une famille dont le père est décédé, il explique être parti pour aider ses proches. Après environ dix-huit mois en Guinée, il dit avoir conservé quelque 100 000 francs CFA d’économies, en plus des sommes envoyées à sa famille et des dépenses de séjour. L’or permettait de vivre, avec des gains irréguliers. Ayouba Wattara avait fait venir son épouse, qui participait au tamisage des résidus. Ce père de famille explique que les revenus agricoles suffisaient difficilement aux besoins du ménage. Son parcours rappelle que les sites aurifères accueillent aussi des familles, avec des besoins de logement, de santé et de protection des enfants. Pour le sociologue Bréhima Ely Dicko, ces déplacements participent à la diversification des revenus. Les réussites visibles entretiennent l’attractivité de l’or. Un départ précipité peut aussi laisser des prêts entre travailleurs sans règlement et priver les proches de ressources attendues. Le préjudice touche ainsi un ensemble de relations économiques et familiales. Le juriste Soumaïla Lah souligne une autre réalité : certains orpailleurs cultivent pendant l’hivernage et cherchent dans l’or un revenu de saison sèche. L’accompagnement gagne à tenir compte de cette complémentarité. Une activité de remplacement aura davantage de chances d’être adoptée si elle répond au calendrier et aux besoins du ménage. Règles Le Mali connaît lui-même le poids de cette économie. Une étude de l’Observatoire du développement humain durable et de lutte contre la pauvreté (ODHD/LCP), relayée par l’Institut national de la statistique (INSTAT), estime la production artisanale à 15,99 tonnes pour la campagne 2024-2025, d’une valeur marchande de 698 milliards de francs CFA. Sur les sites étudiés, 77,9% utilisaient des substances toxiques. Les revenus procurés s’accompagnent donc de coûts environnementaux. Reprendre l’orpaillage suppose un cadre précis. Soumaïla Lah distingue la liberté de circulation des conditions d’exploitation : un séjour régulier ne vaut pas autorisation minière. Le Code de 2023 réserve le permis d’exploitation artisanale aux Maliens et aux ressortissants de pays accordant la réciprocité aux Maliens. La collectivité territoriale le délivre après avis technique des services des Pines, dans un couloir autorisé. Le mercure, le cyanure et le travail des enfants sont interdits. En mars 2025, le chef de l’État avait également ordonné la suspension des permis d’exploitation artisanale accordés à des ressortissants étrangers. Pour le juriste, l’encadrement passe par des sites légalement accessibles, des démarches simplifiées et des circuits d’achat suffisamment rémunérateurs. Il propose aussi des équipements de protection et des moyens de traitement sans mercure. « La formalisation n’avancera que si elle rapporte davantage qu’elle ne coûte », résume-t-il. Cette approche lie l’amélioration des revenus au respect des règles. Accompagnement L’autre possibilité est la reconversion. L’anthropologue Almamy Sylla insiste sur l’écoute des personnes concernées et leur participation au choix des projets. Les compétences, les aspirations et les possibilités économiques locales orientent la réponse. Une activité choisie avec ses bénéficiaires, puis accompagnée après le financement, offre davantage de perspectives qu’une installation décidée à leur place. Bréhima Ely Dicko évoque des formations au carrelage, à l’électricité ou à la plomberie, associées à du matériel et à un fonds de démarrage, avec la possibilité de travailler en coopérative. Certains ont d’abord besoin de soins ou d’un soutien psychosocial. Il recommande également de considérer les jeunes restés sur place et confrontés à des difficultés comparables, afin de limiter les frustrations dans les communautés d’accueil. Les expériences antérieures fournissent des enseignements. Le chercheur rappelle les dispositifs d’aide au retour et de réinsertion liés à l’Office français de l’immigration et de l’intégration (OFII), pour des migrants revenus de France, avec études de faisabilité et suivi des projets. Il relève des difficultés de pérennisation de certains projets individuels. Le financement initial appelle un accompagnement commercial et technique dans la durée. Le temps de formation pose lui-même une difficulté : pendant l’apprentissage, les bénéficiaires ont toujours des proches à nourrir. Une étude publiée en 2021 par le Processus de Rabat relevait déjà ce besoin de revenus immédiats. En février 2026, le ministère chargé des Maliens de l’extérieur et l’Organisation internationale pour les migrations (OIM) ont remis des kits professionnels à des migrants de retour à Kayes. En octobre, un programme national a annoncé 121 millions de francs CFA pour financer 90 projets, notamment agricoles, commerciaux et artisanaux. Ces interventions précèdent la crise guinéenne et concernent des bénéficiaires sélectionnés. Dans L’Essor , Lassine Kondo, revenu de Mauritanie, témoigne d’un appui de 1,5 million de francs CFA reçu en 2025 pour ouvrir un atelier de menuiserie métallique. Il affirme que ses revenus ont doublé. Coopération Adapter ces expériences suppose d’identifier les parcours : Maliens revenus au pays, étrangers souhaitant regagner le leur, travailleurs et familles accompagnantes. Soumaïla Lah propose de relever, pour chacun, la commune d’origine, les compétences, la situation familiale et le projet professionnel. L’insécurité dans certaines localités d’origine complique aussi les perspectives de réinstallation, observe Bréhima Ely Dicko. Le choix d’une activité dépendra du lieu où elle pourra réellement s’exercer. La coordination entre États prend ici toute sa portée. Pour Soumaïla Lah, les fermetures relèvent de la souveraineté nationale, tandis que leurs conséquences humaines franchissent les frontières. Anticiper les déplacements, partager les informations et préparer l’accueil permettrait de mieux articuler protection de l’environnement et protection des personnes. Dans une contribution adressée au journal, Moctar Ousmane Sy appelle à investir dans l’emploi, l’agriculture, la formation et l’entrepreneuriat. « Nous sommes nous-mêmes un pays d’orpaillage », rappelle-t-il. Au Mali comme chez ses voisins, l’enjeu associe la préservation des ressources aux moyens d’existence de ceux qui en vivent. Pour Emmanuel, cette perspective reste concrète : retrouver une activité afin de reconstruire son avenir. La possibilité de gagner durablement leur vie déterminera, pour ces travailleurs et leurs familles, la suite du retour. Massiré Diop

items.title: TPI de Kindia : 23 affaires criminelles jugées en trois jours, dont 13 cas de viol
items.description: Les audiences criminelles ont débuté ce mercredi 18 novembre 2026 au Tribunal de première instance (TPI) de Kindia, en présence de nombreux citoyens et acteurs de la société civile. Au total, 23 dossiers criminels sont inscrits au rôle, dont 13 affaires de viol. Une programmation qui vise notamment à désengorger la Maison centrale de Kindia et à permettre aux différentes parties de faire valoir leurs droits. Prévues pour durer trois jours, ces audiences accordent une place importante aux affaires de violences basées sur le genre (VBG). Interrogé à cette occasion, le substitut du procureur près le TPI de Kindia a expliqué les motivations de cette programmation. « Ce mercredi 18 novembre 2026, le parquet du Tribunal de première instance de Kindia a pris l’initiative, dans la logique de désengorger la Maison centrale, de programmer 23 dossiers criminels. Parmi ces dossiers, le viol occupe une grande place, avec 11 affaires sur les 23. Les autres dossiers concernent notamment des faits d’assassinat et de vol à main armée. Le message que le tribunal entend envoyer, même si les décisions ne sont pas encore rendues, est un appel à accompagner la justice dans la lutte contre la montée de la criminalité, notamment les violences sexuelles. Le ministère public ne ménagera aucun effort pour poursuivre ceux qui ont choisi de s’en prendre aux femmes », a-t-il déclaré. La première affaire examinée a porté sur la comparution de Kêlèty Condé, poursuivi pour des faits de viol sur sa petite amie, qui remonteraient à 2024. À la barre, l’accusé a reconnu avoir entretenu des rapports sexuels avec la plaignante, tout en soutenant que ceux-ci étaient consentis. Selon sa version des faits, la jeune femme s’était rendue chez lui de son propre gré. Après leur rapport intime, il affirme l’avoir raccompagnée avant d’être informé par l’oncle de cette dernière des accusations de viol portées contre lui. De son côté, la partie civile a contesté la version de l’accusé, évoquant une absence de consentement ainsi qu’une défloration. Elle a toutefois reconnu entretenir une relation amoureuse avec le prévenu depuis longtemps. À l’issue des débats, le ministère public a requis cinq ans d’emprisonnement ferme contre Kêlèty Condé et demandé qu’il soit déclaré coupable des faits qui lui sont reprochés. Une réquisition contestée par la défense, qui a plaidé en faveur de circonstances atténuantes, en mettant notamment en avant les éléments qu’elle estime favorables à son client. L’avocat a ainsi demandé au tribunal de limiter la peine à la période déjà passée par l’accusé en détention. Après les différentes plaidoiries, le président du tribunal a renvoyé l’affaire au 20 novembre prochain pour le délibéré et le prononcé du verdict. Aboubacar Dramé, correspondant régional à Kindia +224 623 08 09 10 L’article TPI de Kindia : 23 affaires criminelles jugées en trois jours, dont 13 cas de viol est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .
